docs.title: Meta-Evolve
docs.text:
Meta-Evolve is a declarative Python library for evaluated evolution over versioned artifacts. Start one bounded job with plain callables, then inspect the complete causal record.

Get started Examples API reference

docs.title: One complete support job
docs.text:
This is the exact tested source used by the first-evolution guide:

import meta_evolve as meta


SEED = "I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'm looking into it."


def propose(_parent):
    return "I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'll submit a $49 refund today; it should appear in 5–7 business days."


def grade(reply):
    checks = ("#4021" in reply, "$49" in reply and "refund" in reply.lower(), "already refunded" not in reply.lower() and "refund is complete" not in reply.lower())
    return sum(checks) / len(checks)


result = meta.improve(seed=SEED, proposer=propose, evaluator=grade, trials=1)
print(result.best())


uv run python examples/learn/support_response/quickstart.py
Output
I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'll submit a $49 refund today; it should appear in 5–7 business days.

The seed is evaluated as the baseline. The proposer creates a successor, the independent evaluator checks it, and trials bounds the work. The returned Run records the winner, every attempt, lineage, evidence, usage, stop reason, and declarations. Selecting a result never deploys it.

docs.title: Why Meta-Evolve?
docs.text: Use Meta-Evolve when the improvement loop itself must be programmable and its decisions must remain inspectable: independent evaluation, exact budgets, causal lineage, typed failures, and durable replay apply whichever proposer, search policy, artifact domain, or infrastructure adapter you choose. See how Meta-Evolve compares with optimizer libraries and managed discovery services.

docs.title: Adding an artifact domain
docs.text:
Status: Shipped.

meta.run optimizes whatever you can encode. A domain is one (kind, representation) pair plus the codec that translates between the Python value your proposer and evaluator handle and the durable payload the kernel commits. Adding one takes four small pieces and no change to the library: the coordinator has no branch per domain, which tests/test_four_domain_kernel.py proves by driving number, text, repository, and skill-set runs through one meta.run call site and asserting the same kernel record for all four.

Piece What it is Shipped example Value type what proposers and evaluators see; declares KIND and REPRESENTATION meta.Text Codec encode value → payload, decode payload → value TextCodec Registration Registry.register_artifact_type(codec) built-in codecs skip this Declaration Task(artifact=YourType)

Text is the smallest complete instance and is worth reading first: the value type and its codec are about fifteen lines each. This page builds a second domain — recipe, an ordered list of instruction steps — the same way.

The contracts themselves are canonical elsewhere and are not restated here. ArtifactCodec owns the codec laws, the programming model owns Task, Registry, and meta.run, and the architecture owns what artifacts, kinds, and representations mean.

Every Python block below is one script, run end to end by tests/test_add_a_domain_tutorial.py.

docs.title: 0. Kind and representation
docs.text:
The kind names the schema — what a payload means. The representation names the storage shape that payload is written in. The two are separate because kinds can share a representation: source-tree and skill-set are both utf8-tree-v1, the same portable tree bytes read under different rules. The kind, never the bytes, decides which codec reads a committed payload.

import meta_evolve as meta

print("built-in text domain:", meta.Text.KIND, meta.Text.REPRESENTATION)

docs.title: 1. The value type
docs.text:
Declare KIND and REPRESENTATION as strings on the type; Task(artifact=...) reads exactly those two attributes and nothing else, so a plain class works and no base class is imposed. Subclass whatever Python shape the domain already is — Text is a str, Recipe is a tuple.

Rules that decide whether a value is one of these belong here, in the constructor. Rules about whether a value is any good belong to the evaluator.

from typing import ClassVar


class Recipe(tuple):
    """An ordered sequence of instruction steps."""

    KIND: ClassVar[str] = "recipe"
    REPRESENTATION: ClassVar[str] = "json-steps-v1"

    __slots__ = ()

    def __new__(cls, steps=()):
        steps = tuple(steps)
        if not all(isinstance(step, str) and step.strip() for step in steps):
            raise ValueError("every recipe step must be non-blank text")
        return super().__new__(cls, steps)

docs.title: 2. The codec
docs.text:
encode and decode must be pure, deterministic, and free of I/O, and decode is the only validation entry point — a codec has no separate validate. Return any payload freeze accepts: None, bool, int, finite float, str, lists and tuples of those, and string-keyed mappings of those. Artifact freezes what you return and derives the content digest from it, so codecs never mint or check identity.

Refuse a value that is not yours by raising TypeError or ValueError. Those two are the rejection signal and nothing else is: encode is reached by every proposed candidate as well as by the seed, so a refusal there fails that one trial as a typed InvalidOutput and the run continues, while any other exception is treated as a bug in the codec and propagates.

class RecipeCodec:
    """Translates ``Recipe`` values to and from their durable payload."""

    kind = Recipe.KIND
    representation = Recipe.REPRESENTATION
    interfaces = ("ordered-steps/v1",)

    def encode(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, Recipe):
            raise TypeError("recipe tasks require a Recipe value")
        return tuple(value)

    def decode(self, payload):
        return Recipe(payload)

interfaces names what a consumer may rely on, independently of the kind, so a later artifact carrying the same structure can declare the same interface and reuse its consumers. Leave it () when nothing consumes the domain structurally yet. kind, representation, and every interface name are identity declarations: each must be non-empty and have no outer whitespace. Registration rejects invalid declarations rather than trimming them.

docs.title: 3. Register the codec
docs.text:
registry = meta.Registry()
registry.register_artifact_type(RecipeCodec())
print("declared interfaces:", registry.artifact_interfaces("recipe", "json-steps-v1"))

Registration is keyed by (kind, representation). The six built-in keys are not overridable — changing the decode of an old key would change the meaning of every artifact already committed under it — so a different behavior needs a different key. A new representation of a built-in kind is a different key and registers normally.

docs.title: 4. Declare it on the task and run
docs.text:
Pass the registry to meta.run and name the value type on the task. From here nothing is domain-specific: the proposer receives decoded values and returns one, the evaluator scores one, and search, budgets, lineage, and experience behave exactly as they do for integers.

def add_step(parent, context):
    return Recipe((*parent, f"step {len(parent) + 1}"))


def score(candidate):
    return {"score": float(len(candidate))}


experiment = meta.Experiment(
    task=meta.Task(
        evaluator=score,
        artifact=Recipe,
        budget=meta.Budget(evaluations=4, trials=3),
    ),
    seed=Recipe(("preheat the oven",)),
    proposer=add_step,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=3),
    registry=registry,
)
result = meta.run(experiment)

best = result.best()
print("committed as:", best.kind, best.representation)
print("decoded type:", type(best.value).__name__)
print("best value:", tuple(best.value))
print("primary score:", result.summary().primary_score)

built-in text domain: text utf8-text-v1
declared interfaces: ('ordered-steps/v1',)
committed as: recipe json-steps-v1
decoded type: Recipe
best value: ('preheat the oven', 'step 2', 'step 3', 'step 4')
primary score: 4.0

That is the whole domain. The script imports meta_evolve and the standard library, and touches no library file.

docs.title: 5. Check the codec against the published suite
docs.text:
meta_evolve.conformance.ArtifactCodecTests checks both round trips, repeated-call stability within one process, common file/socket entry points, TypeError/ValueError rejection of foreign values and of malformed payloads (rejected_payloads — decode is validation), decoding through the kernel's CodecIndex, and — for values declared in mutable_values — that a decoded value is independent of the one you encoded. No law compares values with ==: observations go through value_state, whose default knows exact canonical and kernel types only. Recipe subclasses tuple, so its suite overrides value_state with tuple(value) — an observation the codec has no hand in. The I/O patches are tripwires, not proof of arbitrary purity, and repeated calls do not prove cross-process reproducibility. Subclass the suite and override five fixtures (plus value_state for your own value types and mutate if any value is mutable); the published-conformance section of the extensions guide has the snippet and the install extra. RecipeCodec above is checked that way in this tutorial's own test.

Every component family a registered domain composes with — codecs, repository-editing proposers, evaluators, search programs, context policies, workspaces, sandboxes, and typed mutation surfaces — has a published subclassable suite; see meta_evolve.conformance for what each deliberately leaves unchecked.

docs.title: What a registered domain does not get yet
docs.text: • Restart-resumable execution. mode="durable-local" fails closed with CapabilityError for any task whose (kind, representation) is not one of the six built-in keys. A registered codec is a live object rather than registered source, so it carries no manifest and a resumed run could not verify that the code rebuilding a payload is the code that wrote it. Custom domains are local mode in Milestone 7. They may still use durable storage: after reopening the storage and reconstructing the registry, inspect one through meta.Run(run_id, storage, registry=registry). This is decoding only, not resume or execution authority; command-line inspection remains built-in-only.

docs.title: One domain loop
docs.text:
Task → Seed → Proposal → Successor → Evaluation → Search decision
                         └────────→ typed failure

Meta-Evolve evaluates proposed successors to immutable, versioned artifacts. The domain meaning is independent of artifact kind, provider, evaluator, search policy, and storage backend.

docs.title: Layers and dependency direction
docs.text:
Public API    declarations, execution, inspection
Application   normalization, coordination, comparison, replay
Domain        immutable identities, outcomes, evidence, budgets
Ports         proposer, evaluator, search, experience, workspace, storage
Adapters      callables, subprocesses, files, SQLite, user-owned SDKs

Dependencies point inward. Adapters translate external systems at the edge. The coordinator never branches on a provider, artifact kind, evaluator, policy, or infrastructure implementation.

docs.title: Identity and lineage
docs.text:
Content identity and occurrence identity are distinct. Equal bytes may occupy different causal positions and retain different occurrence IDs and parent links. Task, run, proposal, trial, evaluation, evidence, decision, and component identities are not collapsed for storage convenience.

Every successor names its parents. Every decision-relevant observation has a logical time. Durable state is a projection of immutable committed facts, not a mutable workspace, cache, branch, or provider conversation.

docs.title: Authority boundaries
docs.text:
Candidates control only proposed artifact content and authorized derivation. Experiment owners control tasks, evaluators, seeds, data splits, environments, and budgets. Governance controls permissions, visibility, admission, and promotion.

Search may select a best measured artifact; selection grants no deployment authority. A candidate cannot alter hidden evaluation, widen a budget, grant itself experience, erase failures, rewrite audit history, or promote itself.

docs.title: Evaluation and failures
docs.text:
Evaluation is independent of candidate claims. A successful evaluation records finite measurements plus optional evidence, uncertainty, environment identity, and exact usage. Valid poor work remains rankable.

Invalid output, proposer failure, evaluator failure, timeout, resource exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure retain distinct typed semantics. An outcome without a valid measurement is never ranked as a low score. Query refusal such as NoSuccessfulEvaluation is separate from the recorded failures that explain it.

docs.title: Budgets, usage, and randomness
docs.text:
The coordinator owns trial and evaluation accounting. Seed evaluation consumes one evaluation and no successor trial. Tokens, monetary spend, wall time, and experience access are charged to the work that caused them.

A run overlay may narrow but never widen its task budget. Monetary P1 enforces committed spend_micros post hoc; reservation and settlement remain part of unshipped distributed work. Named random streams, deterministic tie rules, and recorded decisions reconstruct local trajectories. External calls are reproducible to their committed transcript and declarations, not promised to regenerate identical bytes.

docs.title: Experience and source visibility
docs.text:
Experience is explicit and off by default. Pushed context is selected, bounded, and committed before proposal. Pulled experience is capability-bounded and audited. Declared derivation may cite only successful, strictly prior, authorized observations.

M8.7 source operations resolve exact same-task/run artifact occurrences through read-only storage, fail closed on invalid targets, charge bounded results, and replay from committed observations. Its optional Git view is disposable adapter metadata, not artifact identity or ambient repository authority. Whole-tree reads, semantic retrieval, persistent Git identity, and cross-run access remain outside the shipped M8.7 contract.

docs.title: Workspaces and execution
docs.text:
Repository proposers receive a private mutable workspace materialized from an immutable artifact. Cleanup occurs before successful capture creates one new immutable occurrence. Evaluators materialize candidates independently and own their commands, hidden graders, environments, and failure translation.

The built-in development subprocess controls limits and process groups; it is not a hardened security boundary. Production isolation belongs to a conforming user-owned sandbox, container, VM, or worker.

docs.title: Durability and replay
docs.text:
Artifacts and append-only transitions are durable truth. Reopening is a read-only projection. Resume verifies component manifests and the recovery frontier, then performs only missing logical work. Replay never reruns a proposer, evaluator, search policy, context selector, or provider.

A session fixes authority, components, and effective budget at start. Each step commits one new decision or completes work already owed by recovery. Lifecycle and rankability remain separate: a stopped run may be unrankable, while an incomplete run may already contain rankable evaluations.

docs.title: Search and archives
docs.text:
Search consumes projected state and emits validated decisions; it never mutates a projection directly. Policy state must be derivable from committed facts. Archive membership is explicit and ordered. Failed evaluations remain scoreless rather than receiving manufactured utilities. Preset-specific selection and tie rules belong to Choose search, not the coordinator.

Fair comparison requires compatible measuring conditions and effective budgets. Allowed treatment differences are reported. Structural compatibility is necessary but does not prove statistical generality or transfer.

docs.title: Typed composite and nested artifacts
docs.text:
Successor validation occurs after encoding and before artifact creation. A codec may restrict mutable surfaces without granting the proposer authority over fixed declarations. Harness and policy candidates cannot change hidden evaluation, split membership, permissions, budgets, or promotion.

Nested evaluators preserve each inner run's identity, lineage, failures, evidence, and usage. Inner trial/evaluation counts remain inner. Captured token, spend, and elapsed usage may roll up once at the outer boundary. Held-out work starts outside development history, and comparison reports eligibility rather than performing promotion.

docs.title: Presentation
docs.text: Artifact presentation reads frozen payloads into bounded inert records. It never executes decoded content. Canonical attachments retain exact bytes; direct-parent diffs retain occurrence context. The loopback browser uses read-only storage and exposes no execution, resume, cancellation, promotion, deletion, or remote-control authority.

docs.title: Replaceability and conformance
docs.text: An independently testable port appears only when a current acceptance gate needs the seam. Published conformance suites cover codecs, proposers, evaluators, search programs, context policies, experience access, workspaces, sandboxes, and mutation surfaces. Storage adapters retain an internal contract. A conformance suite states what it proves and what remains the adapter owner's responsibility.

docs.title: Stable invariants
docs.text:
• Artifacts are immutable; equal content does not collapse causal occurrences.
  • Parent lineage, component identity, randomness, evidence, and usage are explicit.
  • Candidates cannot control evaluation, budgets, permissions, or promotion.
  • Failures without valid measurements are never ranked as low scores.
  • Replay projects committed facts without external execution.
  • Comparisons fail closed when protected declarations differ.
  • Replaceable components enter through ports, never coordinator special cases.

docs.title: How Meta-Evolve compares
docs.text:
This page answers a question new readers ask first: AlphaEvolve, GEPA's optimize_anything, and Meta-Evolve all run "propose, evaluate, keep the better one" loops — so what is actually different, and when would you pick each?

Claims about external systems belong to those systems and reflect their public materials as of August 2026. Nothing here implies Meta-Evolve has reproduced their results.

docs.title: One sentence each
docs.text:
• AlphaEvolve is Google DeepMind's hosted discovery service: you bring a problem and an automated evaluator, Google brings the coding agent, the search, and the compute. Proprietary; generally available on Google Cloud since July 2026.
  • GEPA's optimize_anything is an open-source (MIT) optimizer: a strong reflective-mutation algorithm with Pareto selection, packaged behind a deliberately tiny API — a seed plus an evaluator.
  • Meta-Evolve is an open kernel: a programming model for building your own evaluated improvement loop out of replaceable parts, where every run leaves a durable, replayable, budget-exact record.

All three run the same loop shape. They sell different layers of it:

                 AlphaEvolve   optimize_anything   Meta-Evolve
the results      product       headline            not yet demonstrated
the algorithm    internal      product             simple presets
the loop itself  internal      internal            product

AlphaEvolve's product is the results (you rent the whole system). GEPA's product is the algorithm (the loop is fixed; you feed it). Meta-Evolve's product is the loop itself (you program it; the kernel guarantees the record).

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: AlphaEvolve optimize_anything Meta-Evolve What it is Managed cloud service Optimizer library Loop kernel/library You provide Problem + evaluator Seed + evaluator Task, seed, proposer, search It provides Agent, search, compute Reflection + Pareto search Records, lineage, budgets, replay, seams Candidate form Code Text (string or named strings) Typed artifacts with codecs LLM proposer Built in (Gemini) Built in (your model choice) Not bundled; user-owned callable Loop internals Closed Fixed inside optimize() Every stage replaceable Open source No Yes (MIT) Yes (Apache-2.0)

docs.title: What "control" means here, concretely
docs.text:
Many frameworks are "flexible" through configuration flags. Meta-Evolve is different in a specific way: the loop is programmed, not configured. Each stage — proposer, evaluator, search program, context policy, artifact codec, workspace, storage — is a seam with a published contract and a conformance suite. You swap implementations, not flags.

The practical payoff is ablation. Because a component can be replaced without touching anything else, you can run the identical task several ways under equal budgets and compare the records:

task = meta.Task(evaluator=score_candidate)

for context in (meta.NoMemory(), meta.AncestorsOnly(), meta.PullAccess()):
    experiment = meta.Experiment(
        task=task,
        seed=seed,
        proposer=improve,
        search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=20),
        context=context,
    )
    result = meta.run(experiment)
    print(type(context).__name__, result.best(), result.experience_usage())

That is a controlled experiment on the loop's own memory policy: same task, same proposer, same budget, one variable changed. The experience-reuse example runs exactly this comparison. The same move works for search (Greedy vs BestOfN vs Population — see the policy comparison) and for proposers.

A monolithic optimizer cannot ablate itself this way. In optimize_anything, reflection and Pareto selection live inside the loop; there is no seam at which to remove or replace one of them while holding the rest fixed. That is not a defect — it is the price of a two-argument API — but it means questions like "did the memory help?" or "was it the selection rule or the mutation?" are answerable in Meta-Evolve and not from inside a sealed loop.

docs.title: Control is half; the record is the other half
docs.text:
Swappable parts alone would just be do-it-yourself. The second half is that whatever you plug in, the kernel still enforces the same invariants:

  • Independent evaluation. The evaluator measures the candidate outside the proposer's authority. A candidate cannot grade itself, widen its own budget, erase failures, or promote itself (architecture: authority boundaries).
  • Exact budgets. Seed evaluation, successor attempts, and experience access charge declared budget dimensions exactly, so "equal budget" comparisons are equal by construction, not by convention.
  • Lineage. Every successor names its parents; every decision-relevant observation is recorded at a logical time. run.lineage() is the exact causal chain, and proposers can declare which prior records they used through derived_from.
  • Replay. A durable run can be reopened and replayed to a byte-identical event stream (crash-recovery example). Stated precisely: replay reproduces the recorded run exactly; it does not re-execute a stochastic model. That is what a reviewer needs to check a claim, and it is the part most optimizer libraries do not attempt.

Text-only optimizers also collapse artifact structure into strings: a candidate is well-formed only if the evaluator happens to reject malformed text at scoring time. Meta-Evolve artifacts are typed — source trees take exact-file patches through private workspaces, skill sets and harnesses have declared interfaces — and successors are validated against their parent before commit (add a domain).

docs.title: What the others do better
docs.text:
Honesty in both directions:

  • Call-site simplicity. optimize_anything is a seed and an evaluator. A first Meta-Evolve run asks for five declarations. For "make this prompt better this afternoon," the smaller API is simply the better tool, and the determinism ceremony here is friction with no payoff.
  • A strong proposer out of the box. GEPA ships state-of-the-art reflective mutation; AlphaEvolve ships a frontier coding agent. Meta-Evolve deliberately bundles no model — the shipped presets are simple, and the intelligence is whatever you connect at the proposer seam.
  • Demonstrated results. AlphaEvolve and GEPA lead with headline numbers. Meta-Evolve's examples are deterministic teaching loops; it has not yet produced a live optimization result of its own. Its claims are about the loop's guarantees, not about optimization performance.

docs.title: Choosing in practice
docs.text:
• Improving one prompt or config quickly, cheap evaluations, nobody will audit the run → optimize_anything.
  • Enterprise code optimization with managed compute and no infrastructure appetite → AlphaEvolve on Google Cloud.
  • Controlled experiments on the loop itself (memory, search, proposer ablations), expensive or noisy evaluations where crash recovery and exact accounting matter, bi-level autoresearch setups, or any run whose record must justify a promotion decision → Meta-Evolve.

docs.title: Using them together
docs.text:
These tools compose rather than compete. GEPA-style reflective mutation is, from Meta-Evolve's point of view, a proposer: a callable that reads the parent and prior evidence and returns a ProposalResult (SDK integration). Pareto-frontier retention is a search program behind the same contract as Greedy and Population (extensions). Hosted that way, the optimizer keeps its intelligence and the kernel adds lineage, budgets, and replay.

The same seams make Meta-Evolve usable as a neutral harness for comparing optimizers under exactly equal budgets on identical records — a comparison no single optimizer can run on itself from the inside. Adapter compatibility with existing frameworks is the stated preference over duplicating their APIs; see OpenEvolve in the references.

docs.title: Trace one run through the kernel
docs.text:
Run the canonical example once, then keep its two output lines in view:

uv run python examples/learn/number_search/main.py

12
[0, 1, 2, 7, 12]

The short script enters one coordinator. The actual order is interleaved:

declaration
  → encode, evaluate, and atomically commit the seed
  → search decision and commit
  → proposal, candidate encoding, and commit
  → independent evaluation and commit
  → repeat until the committed stop decision
  → reopen the committed stream as a read-only Run

No stage branches on “number.” The codec handles representation, the proposer handles mutation, the evaluator handles measurement, and search handles the next decision.

docs.title: 1. Declaration
docs.text:
examples/learn/number_search/main.py declares the task, seed, proposer, search preset, budget, and random seed. The root meta.run export reaches application/runtime.py.

runtime.run validates the public values, chooses the codec index, computes the effective budget, adapts callables, checks capabilities, prepares search, and derives the run and task identities. Durable-local validation finishes before the coordinator can write an event.

docs.title: 2. Encoding
docs.text:
The seed is encoded immediately through CodecIndex.encode. A successor stays a Python value while the proposer works; the one place it becomes a durable payload is proposal_completion.py.

A codec's TypeError or ValueError means invalid candidate output and becomes a typed failure. Another exception is a codec defect and propagates. Codecs do not choose artifact IDs, parents, scores, or promotion.

docs.title: 3. Proposal
docs.text:
execution.py loads only the committed parent artifacts named by the trial. It builds a ProposerContext from recorded randomness, logical step, objectives, bounded context, and audited experience, then calls the replaceable proposer runner.

proposal_completion.py checks usage and derivation authority before accepting the candidate. Core code creates the proposal, artifact occurrence, stable IDs, parent links, and provenance. The proposer supplies content and evidence; it does not mint durable identity.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation
docs.text:
evaluation_execution.py decodes the committed artifact and calls the evaluator. Core code adds one evaluation charge, enforces effective budgets, creates stable evidence and evaluation IDs, and records either metrics or a typed failure.

The evaluator is outside candidate authority. A candidate can fail a task and receive a real low score. A broken evaluator, exhausted resource, or infrastructure fault carries no metric and cannot be ranked as poor candidate performance.

docs.title: 5. Search
docs.text:
run_support.py contains the small drive loop. A prepared policy reads only committed SearchState, returns a trial or stop decision, and the coordinator commits the decision before executing a trial.

Greedy's parent choice and retention rules live in policies/greedy.py, not in the coordinator. This is why BestOfN, Population, and a conforming custom policy use the same execution path.

docs.title: 6. Commitment
docs.text:
coordinator.py funnels every durable fact through commit_batch. It first folds the proposed events on a local projection and checks the same batch grammar recovery uses. Storage.commit then writes events and artifact occurrences together. Only a successful store commit advances the in-memory projection.

The seed follows the same rule through bootstrap.py: its declaration, occurrence, trial outcome, evidence, and evaluation form one genesis batch. A partial genesis is never a run.

docs.title: 7. Projection
docs.text:
projections.py rebuilds RunProjection by folding the ordered event stream. Replay consumes records; it never reruns the proposer, evaluator, context selector, or search policy.

results.py projects read-only best, trials, lineage, summary, and comparison views. The printed lineage follows committed artifact parent IDs. It omits rejected 16 because that occurrence is not an ancestor of the winning 12.

docs.title: Authority
docs.text: In proposal_completion.py, list the fields copied from proposer output and the fields minted by core. Explain why moving artifact ID creation into the proposer would let a candidate overwrite history.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: Change only random_seed in a temporary number-search run. Predict which run identity changes and which task identity stays fixed. Then find both inputs in runtime.py and run_support.py.

docs.title: Lineage
docs.text: Sketch the parent IDs for attempts 1, 6, 11, 16, and 12. Explain why two artifact occurrences with equal payload bytes still need distinct IDs.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text: Account for the example's six evaluations and five successor trials. Identify where the seed is charged, where proposal usage is checked, and where evaluator usage is checked. No component may widen the effective budget.

docs.title: Typed failures
docs.text: Classify these outcomes: a candidate violates the task, a codec rejects the candidate type, the grader crashes, and a proposer exceeds its resource grant. Only the first can be an ordinary low score.

docs.title: Replay
docs.text: Read commit_batch beside replay_run_projection. Name the shared fold and grammar checks that keep “committed” equivalent to “recoverable.” Explain why replay must not ask the proposer for the same candidate again.

docs.title: Comparison validity
docs.text:
Use the operations lab to compare Greedy and BestOfN. Then list the declarations that must match before the winner is meaningful. A displayed winner is not evidence when task, evaluator, initial artifact, budget, proposer, or hidden component configuration changed.

When you can answer all seven exercises from source, continue to the M8 design capstone.

docs.title: Implementation Plan
docs.text: This document is the technical companion to the canonical milestone roadmap. The roadmap owns implementation order, demonstrations, and acceptance gates. The programming model owns public API signatures. This plan records only the package boundaries, ports, adapters, and technical choices needed to implement each milestone.

docs.title: Pre-milestone API spike
docs.text:
Status: Shipped. The spike lives under experiments/00_api_spike/ and ran both required demonstrations; its ergonomic findings are recorded in real_model_findings.md and reflected in the programming model. The section below is kept as the record of what the spike was scoped to prove.

Before creating the durable package, build a disposable one-to-three-file prototype under experiments/00_api_spike/.

It must run the same target API against:

  1. deterministic integer improvement with greedy and best-of-N search;
  2. a real-model prompt-optimization example with a small callable proposer and evaluator.

The spike may use closures, live objects, and an in-memory list. It does not need events, ports, grants, persistence, or production provider handling. Its purpose is to test whether Task, meta.run, Proposer, Evaluator, SearchProgram, and Run feel coherent in working code.

Treat the implementation as disposable. Feed ergonomic findings back into the programming model, then implement only the justified contracts in Milestone 1.

Domain code contains immutable values and transitions; adapters contain infrastructure; the coordinator depends only on the ports introduced so far.

docs.title: Milestone 1: deterministic in-memory kernel
docs.text: Status: Shipped (July 21, 2026). The exit gate is covered by the canonical number-search example and the retained-event reconstruction acceptance suite. This is event-to-projection replay and built-in decision reproduction, not process restart or resume.

docs.title: Domain records
docs.text:
Implement frozen, serializable models for only the first complete logical loop:

  • Task
  • Artifact
  • Proposal
  • TrialSpec, Trial, and TrialOutcome
  • Evaluation and Evidence
  • SearchDecision, PolicyRef, and OperatorSpec
  • Budget and Usage
  • the minimal typed events and projected SearchState

Trial is the logical experiment. WorkItem is its delivery envelope and stays an internal kernel record: the sequential local coordinator may introduce it when scheduling needs a seam, and it never appears in user-facing types. Do not add leases or retry-attempt identities until distribution requires them.

Use opaque typed identifiers and schema versions on durable envelopes. Keep semantic artifact kind separate from storage representation. Simple integers or strings are normalized through a basic artifact codec rather than special-cased by the coordinator.

Durable foreign references use explicit _id and _ids suffixes. The common artifact envelope exposes kind, representation, schema_version, and parent_ids; Task.artifact_kind names the same semantic classification as Artifact.kind.

docs.title: Minimal ports
docs.text:
class ArtifactStore(Protocol):
    def put(self, artifact: Artifact) -> None: ...
    def get(self, artifact_id: ArtifactId) -> Artifact: ...


class EventStore(Protocol):
    def append(
        self,
        run_id: RunId,
        expected_version: int,
        events: Iterable[EventEnvelope],
    ) -> int: ...

    def read(
        self,
        run_id: RunId,
        after: int = 0,
    ) -> tuple[EventEnvelope, ...]: ...


class Proposer(Protocol):
    def propose(self, parent, context) -> CandidateLike | ProposalResult: ...


class Evaluator(Protocol):
    def evaluate(self, candidate) -> EvaluationLike: ...

Start with callable proposer and evaluator adapters plus in-memory stores. Do not introduce ExperienceGraph, SDK runtime, workspace, sandbox, or SQLite ports in this milestone.

M1.1 deliberately made Artifact responsible for freezing payloads, validating content digests, and carrying occurrence identity. Storage adapters therefore accept complete, already validated artifacts and preserve them as-is instead of reconstructing artifacts from separate payload and metadata arguments.

M1.3 keeps replay as a pure events → SearchState fold. Durable event facts record the run configuration, policy decisions, completed trials, artifact occurrences, and evaluations; the disposable state derives best-so-far, failures, usage, remaining budgets, and decision-scoped randomness through plain properties. Historical budget overages remain replayable and floor projected remaining resources at zero, while Budget.remaining_after retains its strict rejection semantics for prospective accounting. Named seeds and logical decision ids use versioned SHA-256 derivation rather than Python's process-randomized hash.

The M1.3 SearchProgram contract intentionally contains only next(state). Archive composition remains Milestone 2 work. Proposal submission facts, in-flight trial transitions, authority checks, and idempotent completion remain with the callable-adapter and coordinator slices that can establish their full semantics.

M1.4 adds the independently testable callable boundary. Proposer and Evaluator ports operate on decoded Python values, and local callable adapters normalize plain or rich returns into immutable ProposalResult and EvaluationResult records. EvidenceDraft carries validated evidence content before the coordinator assigns identity. Evaluator normalization validates finite metrics, non-negative uncertainty, and coverage of the task objectives; additional diagnostic metrics remain valid, while objective direction stays in the task. Callable-reported tokens, charged monetary spend, and wall time remain attributable to the action, but nonzero trial or evaluation counts are invalid because the coordinator owns those counts. When a returned failure is converted to InvalidOutput — a role-mismatched failure kind or a count violation — the original failure's kind, message, and details are preserved in the invalid output's details. These boundary records are not durable types and do not expand the root public API or serialization allowlist.

M1.5 implements the sequential coordinator and durable conversion. One rich lifecycle projection is the replay validator and derives the smaller policy-facing SearchState. The coordinator commits a causal bootstrap trial without charging a successor attempt, commits successor proposals and artifacts before evaluation, mints evidence identity, preserves lineage across evaluator failure, and accounts for authoritative proposal attempts and evaluator calls.

M1.6 records one durable SearchSpec on RunStarted: the policy reference, frozen declared configuration, and authorized proposer. Internal prepare_search() composes that declaration with the executable program and a deterministic identity key. Presets bind themselves structurally; Greedy.bind owns its mutate operator and unit trial allocation, while already executable custom programs pass through unchanged. This keeps preset-specific binding and identity formatting out of run() and lets retained events reproduce built-in Greedy decisions without adding replay to the root API.

docs.title: Sequential coordinator
docs.text:
while True:
    state = projections.search_state(run_id)
    decision = search.next(state)

    if isinstance(decision, Stop):
        coordinator.stop(decision)
        break

    coordinator.execute(decision)

For a TrialSpec, the coordinator:

  1. validates authority and remaining budget;
  2. derives and records named deterministic random substreams;
  3. commits the stable Trial identity with the decision;
  4. allocates a local WorkItem;
  5. invokes the proposer and commits its proposal before evaluation;
  6. captures the successor artifact occurrence;
  7. commits the execution TrialOutcome and usage;
  8. invokes the evaluator outside candidate authority and records its separate evaluation and evidence.

The seed follows the same causal record chain through a coordinator-owned bootstrap trial at logical step zero. It consumes one evaluation but zero successor trials, so policy logical step one and Greedy.max_trials begin with the first proposer attempt. Projected counts sum the authoritative usage on outcomes and evaluations rather than counting record collections.

Operator policies return typed OperatorSpec values. User-facing string shorthands are normalized before the trial is committed.

docs.title: Reference problem and exit
docs.text:
Use integer search. The same task, initial artifact, root random seed, policy, and budget must produce the same decisions and projected state. Rebuilding a fresh in-memory projection from the retained event list must reproduce the result; process restart and filesystem persistence remain Milestone 4 concerns.

The kernel exits this milestone when trial identity, lineage, budgets, failure taxonomy, deterministic randomness, duplicate completion, replay, and policy replacement have focused tests.

docs.title: Milestone 2: replaceable search policies
docs.text:
M2.1 establishes the shared durable boundary before adding another preset. ArchiveUpdate is a record-only SearchDecision: projection validates its evaluation, candidate, admission or rejection, optional eviction, and complete rank-ordered membership. PolicyDecisionExplained immediately links rationale to a decision without changing the frozen M1 decision or trial schemas.

The runtime commits trials, archive updates, and stops through one application path. Policies may optionally describe a decision and name the random streams they used; the runtime derives the recorded seeds. Deterministic fallbacks keep a custom policy's required contract at next(state) only. The initial shared conformance harness covers Greedy and such a minimal custom policy. Ranking, tournament selection, and composed archive or stopping policies wait for a second concrete use in BestOfN or Population.

M2.2 adds BestOfN(max_trials=20) through the same preset-binding and SearchProgram.next(state) contracts as Greedy. It always expands the seed, uses the derived stable top-1 result view, emits no ArchiveUpdate, and binds a mutate operator with a one-trial, one-evaluation allocation narrowed by remaining budget. Its versioned declaration is best-of-n@1 with frozen max_trials configuration. The bootstrap evaluation participates in ranking but consumes neither a successor trial nor a policy step.

Keep this small implementation parallel to Greedy in M2.2. M2.3 is the extraction checkpoint: Population supplies the third concrete policy shape needed to judge whether shared selection, allocation, stopping, ranking, or archive seams simplify the code. Put Greedy, BestOfN, Population, and a minimal custom policy behind one conformance suite without adding coordinator cases.

M2.3 adds Population(size=3, tournament_size=2, max_trials=20) through the same preset contracts. The extraction checkpoint yielded exactly one shared seam: the private stable-ranking primitive rank_evaluations in the domain, which now backs the incumbent view, the derived result view, and population membership. Selection, allocation, and stopping seams stay inlined; three policies did not justify them. Population processes every evaluation through one record-only ArchiveUpdate before any stop, and draws tournament members from the named selection stream with a self-contained integer draw rather than random.Random, whose sampling algorithm may change across Python versions and would break historical decision reproduction. When no member is admitted it stops with population_empty rather than expanding a non-member seed.

M2.4 completes the milestone with frozen, slotted RunSummary and RunComparison application views. Run.summary() retains only immutable identities, declarations, usage, content references, and frozen payload values; it carries no storage or run-token dependency. Run.compare() rejects every task, primary-objective, budget, initial-artifact, evaluator, and proposer declaration mismatch independently. Policy declarations/configurations and root seeds may differ, and exact primary scores tie without secondary tiebreaking. The views remain outside the durable serialization allowlist.

examples/learn/policy_comparison/ owns the deterministic 40-seed benchmark and aggregation. A tiny main.py executes it under its canonical local callable identity, while an executed notebook presents the full score, evaluation, and usage distributions plus representative topology. Notebook verification uses locked nbconvert tooling and always writes execution output to a temporary file. The companion executed milestone_2_tour.ipynb is the guided entry point for the completed milestone and keeps internal projection inspection explicitly separate from the simple callable path.

The coordinator must not know which policy is active. Selector, Allocator, OperatorPolicy, ArchivePolicy, and StopPolicy may begin as small protocols or values only when at least two implementations justify each seam.

Record each decision's policy version, logical identity, observed state reference, named random substreams, and rationale metadata. Comparisons use equal declared evaluation budgets and deterministic tie-breaking.

docs.title: Milestone 3: shared experience
docs.text:
Add the first experience-specific ports only now:

class ExperienceGraph(Protocol):
    def node(self, ref, query): ...
    def ancestors(self, ref, query): ...
    def children(self, ref, query): ...
    def siblings(self, ref, query): ...
    def frontier(self, query): ...
    def trace(self, ref, query): ...
    def state_at(self, query): ...


class ExperienceReader(Protocol):
    def search(
        self, *, record_kinds=(), failure_kinds=(), as_of=None, limit=None
    ) -> ExperienceObservation: ...
    def open(self, ref, *, as_of=None) -> ExperienceObservation: ...
    def ancestors(
        self, trial_ref, *, as_of=None, limit=None
    ) -> ExperienceObservation: ...
    def siblings(
        self, trial_ref, *, as_of=None, limit=None
    ) -> ExperienceObservation: ...
    def compare(
        self, left_trial_ref, right_trial_ref, *, as_of=None
    ) -> ExperienceComparison: ...

M3.1 is the read-only temporal projection only. It adds durable ExperienceRef(run_id, kind, occurrence_id) values based on existing occurrence identities and immutable ExperienceRecord, trial-centered ExperienceNode, ExperienceQuery(task_id, run_id, as_of), and ExperienceState views. replay_experience_graph() first uses the validated run replay path, then attaches the exact committed decision, explanation, proposal, artifact-creation, outcome, evidence, evaluation, and completed-trial records. It does not change coordinator, event-store, artifact-store, existing identity, or event-byte contracts. The #98 conformance closure later root-exported those four values plus ExperienceGraph as the minimal type-complete, read-only surface needed to implement a third-party ContextPolicy; replay construction stays in meta_evolve.application.

Parent edges follow declared parent artifact occurrences to their producing trials. Relations preserve parent order and deduplicate; returned nodes sort by (logical_step, trial_id). Ancestors exclude self, siblings include self, frontier returns visible causal leaves rather than archive members, and a trace covers the target trial plus its accessible ancestors, with records sorted by event sequence plus a fixed kind order. Historical as_of boundaries are inclusive, including bootstrap step zero.

One private access predicate enforces matching task and run, inclusive logical time, local occurrence, visibility, and synthetic retraction. All inaccessible direct targets raise the same content-free ExperienceAccessDenied; collection queries omit inaccessible nodes and do not cross them. The hidden, retracted, and non-local sets exist only to test the filtering contract. They are not a public policy abstraction and establish no Milestone 12 governance contract.

M3.2 implements NoMemory, AncestorsOnly, and BestSibling with direct max_records=20 and max_chars=8_000 defaults. None and NoMemory() add no declaration, wrapper, identity input, fact, or trial policy. A non-default ContextSpec is the next run-identity input after the M1/M2 segments and is declared after bootstrap. A generic search wrapper stamps its PolicyRef into successor TrialSpec values; a separate generic coordinator operation selects or reloads the exact bundle. No coordinator branch depends on a policy or graph relation.

Without pull access, selection follows PolicyDecisionMade → PolicyDecisionExplained → ContextSelected → ProposalSubmitted; with pull access, grant issuance and audited operations sit between selection and proposal. Replay validates declaration authority, ordering, uniqueness, observed version, strictly prior visible references, and exact source values, then returns the committed bundle without invoking the selector or renderer. Context record/render usage remains separate from task Usage.

M3.3 adds run-level PullAccess, durable ExperienceSpec and per-successor ExperienceGrant, scoped pull operations, exact observations/comparisons, and cumulative ExperienceUsage. The serialized access spec follows any ContextSpec in run identity. None contributes no identity segment, event, grant, reader, or compatibility change.

The local grant fixes task, run, trial, and as_of=logical_step - 1, then enforces operation, result, record, and independently rendered-character bounds. Each structurally valid call commits an attempt before validation and then exactly one success, denial, or exhaustion. Attempt 21 under the default 20-operation limit is charged as operation 21 and audited as exhausted. Successes store the exact returned value; replay holds each success to the shared deterministic contract against committed sources and returns the committed value without re-running live retrieval, traversal, or rendering logic. The reader holds only its grant, a view of its own committed operations, a grant-scoped graph built once per grant, and a trial-bound append capability for the permitted audit facts. Identity and visibility remain single-user stubs. Principal authorization, licensing, and federation policy are deliberately deferred; future-information leakage and observation recording are not.

Evaluate push-only context, pull-only exploration, combined access, and no-memory baselines under equal budgets.

M3.4 adds no new lifecycle event. Durable and callable proposals gain an ordered derived_from tuple whose empty default is canonically omitted. A small application contract reconstructs the trial observation ledger from committed context selections and successful pull results, then serves both live completion and proposal replay. The coordinator applies resource exhaustion, derivation policy, and reported proposer failure in that order.

RunExperienceUsage is a derived application view. It sums committed bundle usage and the final cumulative pull ledger once per grant. RunSummary carries both memory declarations and this projection; RunComparison allows different memory declarations and reports exact equality flags. The canonical examples/learn/experience_reuse/ experiment closes the milestone with all four memory variants under identical non-memory declarations and budgets.

docs.title: Milestone 4: durable local kernel
docs.text: Status: Shipped (July 24, 2026; #4, #47). The implementation uses filesystem content-addressed artifacts, an append-only SQLite event stream, explicit component manifests, atomic storage composition, and shared replay/resume validation.

docs.title: SQLite object and transition store
docs.text:
Store immutable domain objects as normalized append-only records or content-addressed envelopes. Store lifecycle changes in an append-only event ledger. Creation of an object and its corresponding transition event occurs in one transaction.

Add:

  • optimistic event-stream concurrency;
  • durable run, trial, work-item, usage, population, and experience projections;
  • stable idempotency keys and logical steps;
  • exact context bundles and experience-query results;
  • as-of search-state reconstruction;
  • explicit schema versions and migrations.

Object records are authoritative for object content. Events are authoritative for the fact that transitions occurred. Projections are disposable and rebuildable.

docs.title: Filesystem artifact store
docs.text:
.meta-evolve/
├── artifacts/sha256/...
├── runs/...
└── meta-evolve.sqlite

Identical payload bytes reuse content identity while distinct artifact occurrences retain trial, proposal, contributor, and parent lineage.

docs.title: Recovery scenario
docs.text: Terminate a deterministic run at each important transition, reconstruct a new coordinator from disk, resume from committed state, and compare it with an uninterrupted run. Closures are rejected in durable-local mode or cause an explicit capability error before execution; they never silently create a run advertised as resumable.

docs.title: Milestone 5: executable artifacts
docs.text:
Status: Shipped. Milestone 5 is complete through the M5.4 canonical clamp acceptance. The closure adds integrated assertions, an executed tour, and documentation only; it adds no production port, schema, registry, patch format, or authority claim.

M5.1 ships the first synchronous source-workspace vertical:

class WorkspaceProvider(Protocol):
    def materialize(self, artifact: object) -> Workspace: ...
    def capture(self, workspace: Workspace) -> object: ...
    def dispose(self, workspace: Workspace) -> None: ...


class ProposerRunner(Protocol):
    component: ComponentRef
    def validate_run(
        self,
        *,
        artifact_kind: str,
        artifact_representation: str,
        objectives: tuple[Objective, ...],
        budget: Budget,
        experience: ExperienceSpec | None,
    ) -> None: ...
    def execute(
        self,
        parents: tuple[Artifact, ...],
        context: ProposerContext,
    ) -> ProposalResult: ...

SourceTree uses the stable utf8-tree-v1 representation. PatchProposer accepts one exact-file command, while PatchResult carries the same evidence, usage, metadata, failure, and derivation information as an ordinary proposal. A decoded-value runner preserves the original callable path; the coordinator does not branch on either runner.

DirectoryWorkspaces copies immutable source into a fresh private directory, captures through the same source validation, and disposes before result commitment. A disposal failure is an infrastructure failure and prevents success commitment because M5.1 has no honest mixed success-plus-infrastructure-warning outcome.

M5.2 ships the synchronous SandboxProvider, immutable ProcessSpec and ProcessResult, and the clearly named DevelopmentSubprocessSandbox. The POSIX adapter enforces an absolute executable, workspace-contained normalized cwd, exact declared environment, timeout, independent raw-byte output bounds, whole-process-group termination, and lifecycle cleanup. Policy, timeout, resource, and infrastructure failures remain typed; ordinary nonzero exits are not interpreted. Narrow clock and process-operation seams make precedence and cleanup behavior deterministic under test. It makes no claim to secure arbitrary untrusted code. Add Git worktrees only as an optimization.

M5.3 ships CommandEvaluator, EvaluationEnvironment, and root-exported ProcessSpec. The evaluator is a declared local callable component and uses the existing callable-evaluator path. Its digest-backed component version commits the complete command, environment, scoring, adapter, and exit-protocol semantics. Task construction invokes a general optional evaluator validate_task hook after normalization; no concrete evaluator branch enters the coordinator.

The adapter materializes only a SourceTree, runs the declared process, and always disposes the workspace. Exit 0 and 1 produce passing and failing metrics; other exits become EvaluatorFailure. Existing process failures stay typed and non-rankable. Environment and bounded process-result evidence remain separate from metrics, and evaluator usage receives process wall time without claiming coordinator-owned evaluation counts. Cleanup failure overrides prior completion while retaining its classification, evidence, and usage.

The evaluator-owned grader remains outside the candidate mutation surface. The development sandbox still makes no hostile-code filesystem-isolation claim; stronger providers remain replaceable at the same structural port.

M5.4 pins deterministic content digests and semantic outcomes, while treating measured wall time as occurrence data. Reopened durable storage supports best-artifact and lineage queries; cold resume of these local live components fails explicitly and without side effects. SDK-backed proposers now remain user-owned local callables; portable reconstruction of patch, command, and live SDK components remains later work.

The M5-owned file audit splits patch-proposer core behavior from lifecycle/resume failures and sandbox declarations/contracts from process execution. Canonical design documents remain cohesive source-of-truth exceptions to the 300-line guideline, and unrelated pre-M5 suites are not refactored as part of this closure.

docs.title: Milestone 6: SDK proposer boundary proof
docs.text: Status: Shipped. M6 completed on July 28, 2026 by proving that native coding SDKs could participate through the ordinary proposer seam without a provider-shaped coordinator. The first-party adapters and extras were superseded on August 5 in favor of user-owned SDK callables; the obsolete provider capture archive was removed on August 6. This section records only the contract that remains part of the shipped architecture.

docs.title: Retained contract
docs.text:
• ProposerContext carries exact objectives, randomness, pushed context, and an optional scoped experience reader without evaluator, budget, permission, or promotion authority.
  • A structural propose(parent, context) object and a plain callable use the same runner path, validation, typed failures, usage, evidence, and derivation records.
  • SDK authentication, sessions, tools, permissions, retries, structured decoding, and provider telemetry belong to the user-owned wrapper.
  • Meta-Evolve retains candidate validation, external evaluation, effective budgets, durable records, lineage, audited experience, and promotion authority.

docs.title: Removed surface
docs.text:
There are no meta_evolve.claude or meta_evolve.codex modules, provider extras, compatibility shims, provider conformance fixtures, or generic live smoke directory. Current opt-in SDK demonstrations are milestone-owned experiments, such as the M8 harness driver, and add no core dependency.

The retired adapter implementations and live measurements remain recoverable from Git history and the closed M6 issues. They are historical development evidence, not current tests, documentation fixtures, or acceptance gates.

docs.title: Milestone 7: cross-domain local v1
docs.text:
Add the artifact registry and public extension contracts only after number, text, and code examples have exercised them.

The common artifact envelope contains semantic kind, representation, schema, interfaces, payload reference, content digest, parent occurrences, and provenance. Domain names such as TextArtifact, GitTreeArtifact, and SkillSetArtifact are typed constructors or views rather than a required inheritance hierarchy.

M7 P1+P2 formalized the SourceTree payload shape into an explicit codec protocol, ArtifactCodec (ports/codecs.py): every kind, including the default python-value, now resolves through a per-run CodecIndex (application/codecs.py) instead of a hard-coded dispatch. Declared interfaces resolve through the registered codec (Registry.artifact_interfaces), not through a new field on the Artifact envelope, so this added no durable schema bump — CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION is unchanged. Registry.register_artifact_type rejects every codec offered for an already-built-in (kind, representation) key — the built-in object included — so the then-four built-in keys (python-value/canonical-json, source-tree/utf8-tree-v1, text/utf8-text-v1, skill-set/utf8-tree-v1) remain non-overridable. The unit is the key, not the kind: a new representation of a built-in kind is a distinct key and registers like any other custom type.

P3 added skill-set (domain/skill_set.py), the first kind to reuse another kind's representation and the first codec with a non-empty interfaces declaration (skill-documents/v1). SkillSet wraps SourceTree construction and adds one rule, layout: every path matches skills/<name>.md. It carries no manifest — M8's HarnessArtifact defines those against a real consumer — and no content validation, since content meaning belongs to whoever reads the skills. Its codec is a fourth built-in rather than a registered custom type: the durable-local gate exists because a registered codec is a live object with no verifiable manifest, and a codec shipped with the library is verifiable exactly like the other three, so skill-set runs stay durable and resumable. That registration works for third parties is proven separately by tests/test_artifact_type_registry.py.

Proposed candidates route through the same CodecIndex as the seed, in application/proposal_completion.py — the original plan scoped only seed encoding — so a candidate the codec rejects becomes a typed InvalidOutput that fails its trial without raising into the run, and a custom artifact type now works through proposer output as well as input. application/runtime.py's durable-local validation block fails closed with CapabilityError when a task's (kind, representation) is not one of the built-in keys: a registered codec is a live object rather than a source function, so require_source_function cannot reach it, and a resumed run would otherwise rebuild payloads with unverified code.

The codec index is a per-run dependency. application/runtime.py and application/resume.py construct it once and return active results through the private Run._reopen(run_id, storage, codecs) path, preserving the exact codec objects used for that run. The public Run(run_id, storage, *, registry: Registry | None = None) constructor builds a read-only index with CodecIndex.with_extras(registry.artifact_types()) when a registry is supplied, merging its custom codecs with all built-ins while the built-ins retain precedence. This intentionally exposes every codec in that registry to decoding; the replayed run projection still selects the artifact kind read by each query, and the constructor grants no execution or mutation authority. Without a registry it remains the built-in reopening path. Codec declaration validation lives once in registry_support.validate_artifact_codec: kind, representation, and every interface name are non-empty and whitespace-exact, while an empty interface tuple remains valid. Both registry registration and the published codec suite call that same validator.

P4 demonstrated the milestone's exit gate. tests/test_four_domain_kernel.py drives number, text, repository, and skill-set runs through one meta.run call site; everything M7 permits a use case to vary lives in one Domain record, and no assertion is written for a single domain. The four leave an identical kernel record — same event sequence, usage, scores, logical steps, and audited experience — while declaring four distinct kinds over three representations, two of which share utf8-tree-v1. No domain needed a coordinator branch, special case, or workaround, and the phase changed no file under src/: the generality was already there to be measured, which is what makes the result a proof rather than a repair.

The purity allowlists are decisions, not accidents. Two properties are pinned by tests/test_application_purity.py, each with an explicit allowlist whose every member carries its justification in the test file itself, and each with a companion test that fails once a member stops being needed — so an exemption cannot quietly outlive its reason.

  • Imports. Application modules import no concrete adapter except storage.py (composes the default memory/filesystem/sqlite stores), unit_of_work.py (owns the atomic durable commit across both stores), run_support.py (constructs the callable-adapter runners for run and resume), and runtime.py (wires the public run() entry point). All four are wiring: something has to name the concrete implementations a default meta.run composes, and the allowlist exists to keep that set visible and small rather than to excuse it.
  • Type dispatch. Nothing calls isinstance against a concrete artifact type outside application/codecs.py and adapters/. The codec is the artifact-type dispatch — encode must refuse a value of the wrong type before it can become a payload — and adapters translate at the edge, where an external system's output first has to become a declared artifact value or a typed failure. The watched set is derived rather than listed: any class in meta_evolve.domain declaring string KIND and REPRESENTATION — the pair Task(artifact=...) reads — falls under the gate the moment it exists, and a guard test pins the derived set so a fifth artifact type is a visible decision rather than a silent widening.

P5a added the milestone's one new storage surface, the read-only listing Storage.runs() -> tuple[RunId, ...], so the CLI's list verb (and any caller whose ids have left the terminal scrollback) can reach Run, resume, and compare again. Two decisions are worth recording.

Enumeration is an optional capability, not a widened port. EventStore keeps exactly append and read; the listing is a separate one-method protocol, ports.RunIndex, that both bundled stores implement. Both required methods are run-scoped, so an implementation can be addressable without being enumerable — one stream handed in at construction, a backend exposing only GET /runs/{id}/events, a store sharded so that "all runs" spans shards. Requiring enumeration of every implementation would earn complexity from a hypothetical rather than the current gate, and would break the hand-built Storage(artifact_store, event_store) pair that LocalOnlyUnitOfWork exists to serve. Storage.runs() checks isinstance(self.events, RunIndex) and raises CapabilityError otherwise; it never reports a non-enumerable store as an empty one. This follows the is_durable principle — a capability is declared by the component, never inferred from a concrete type — but not its mechanism: durability needs a separate boolean because it is invisible in a commit strategy's method set, whereas here the capability is the method, so implementing it is the declaration and a parallel flag could only disagree with it.

Ids, sorted. The listing returns RunIds rather than a richer record: Run.summary() already owns per-run detail, and a richer listing would force the SQLite backend to decode every envelope just to enumerate. Ordering is lexicographic by id, not insertion — in-memory insertion order is a dict accident and SQLite has no insertion column short of rowid, an implementation detail unstable across VACUUM and interleaved appends. Sorting makes the two backends provably agree, which is the property callers depend on. Run ids are run-<sha256>, so the order carries no chronological meaning and is documented not to.

P5b added meta_evolve.cli and the meta-evolve entry point: five verbs — run, list, inspect, resume, compare — over the same public API, using stdlib argparse, no configuration DSL, and no capability logic of its own. A run takes an experiment module exposing one experiment() factory with no import-time side effects; the command line supplies only --storage and --mode. M10.1 made the factory's return a typed Experiment; dictionary returns remain 1.x compatibility with a DeprecationWarning. list is one verb beyond the milestone's four because run ids are content-derived digests rather than names anyone retypes from memory: without enumeration, every other verb is unreachable once an id leaves the terminal. Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for a domain failure (RunError), and 2 for a usage or experiment-module error; anything else keeps its traceback rather than being flattened into a message.

Closed by the M7 defect-repair pass. compare_runs previously refused two incompatible runs with a bare ValueError from _require_equal (application/comparisons.py), which is not a RunError and so escaped the command line's typed-failure translation, reaching the user as a traceback. _require_equal now raises RunsNotComparable, a RunError carrying the declaration that differed as structured data rather than only in its message. The message text is unchanged, so prose matching still works; the command line now reports it as one error line and exit code 1 like every other typed failure.

The other four decisions of that pass. The surfaces themselves are docs/programming-model.md's; what is recorded here is why each landed the way it did.

  • One accessor, not a second view type. Run.trials() returns the existing TrialView, which gained a state field set from the projection records rather than re-derived from other view fields. failure was deliberately left alone: splitting it is breaking, and it still could not express "unevaluated", which is an authorization outcome rather than a fault. The seed trial is included, because three of the six workarounds it replaced depended on unpacking it.
  • CapabilityError is reserved abort control flow, escaping both the proposer and the evaluator boundary unwrapped. RunError is deliberately not in either escape tuple: a nested evaluator may legitimately hit a RunError subclass while reading its inner run, and a broad escape would turn that into a crashed outer run rather than a typed evaluator failure carrying the usage already incurred. (This rationale once cited three examples calling summary() inside their evaluator; issue #143 moved all three to the failure-safe inspect().overview.task_usage, so that evidence no longer holds even though the decision does.) Because CapabilityError is publicly exported, the contract binds user code and is documented, not merely implemented.
  • The name-only report keys on the run-local version sentinel, never on origin == "local". CommandEvaluator is local-origin and versions itself with a configuration digest; keying on origin would condemn exactly the local comparisons that are controlled. ComponentRef.configured_local refuses that sentinel for the same reason, and derives origin and the retained adapter rather than accepting them, since Task's declaration hook admits a component only when it is local and holds that exact callable by identity.
  • Declarable turn limits keep their existing defaults exactly. The defaults emit byte-identical native profiles, so no component.version and no Claude run id moves. native_profile takes the limit keyword-required instead of choosing between two constants, so a normalizer and a transport cannot silently disagree about what was sent. Rejected: max(requested, PULL_MIN) — silently rewriting a chosen number is the defect class being removed.

P6 published the conformance kit and the tutorial.

Published conformance covers all seven component types. meta_evolve.conformance ships subclassable pytest suites, on the pandas ExtensionArray model, for artifact codecs (ArtifactCodecTests), repository-editing proposers (RepositoryProposerTests, PullRepositoryProposerTests), evaluators (EvaluatorTests), search programs (SearchProgramTests), context policies (ContextPolicyTests), workspaces (WorkspaceProviderTests), and sandboxes (SandboxProviderTests), alongside the MutationSurfaceTests that M8 introduced and M9 generalized to four surfaces.

P6 shipped only the first two. M9 published SearchProgramTests, and the #98 follow-up closed the rest. Three of them existed as function-based suites under tests/ (policy_contract.py, workspace_contract.py, sandbox_contract.py) whose laws were already validated against a second implementation; converting those was exposure, not invention, and the function modules were deleted so a published suite and its retired twin cannot drift. policy_contract.py outlived M9's class suite because that suite took a policy instance, which cannot express a program built around the proposer; SearchProgramTests now takes either an instance or a search_factory, so the function module could go and MinimalPolicy runs through the published suite like everything else.

The two proposer suites are exercised by in-repository reference callables (tests/test_proposer_conformance.py) — no first-party provider adapter ships, and the docs say so rather than implying one. The earlier claim that tests/ covered "both providers" had been false since the user-owned SDK boundary removed those adapters; the reference callables are what make it true again at the level a test can honestly pin. Evaluators and context policies had no reusable suite. ContextPolicyTests derives its laws from what the kernel already enforces, in bundle_violation. ContextPolicy.select receives the root-exported ExperienceGraph, and the query, node, record, and state values its methods exchange are root-exported as one closed read-only surface. Construction through replay_experience_graph remains an internal application service. EvaluatorTests is only partly of that kind: the objective-coverage and typed-failure laws follow adapters/evaluators.py, but stability, order-independence, and non-mutation are not kernel-enforced — they are obligations an evaluator can break today, which is why the suite is where they are stated. Only the store suite stays internal in store_contract.py: store adapters are not one of the seven extension families.

The suites state their limits. ContextPolicyTests does not apply to NoMemory, which meta.run normalizes away before any policy runs, and asks a policy that selects nothing to declare it through expects_records — an empty bundle is accepted by the kernel, so refusing one outright would have been a law the shipped contract does not have. EvaluatorTests skips its typed-failure law visibly when a subclass declares no rejected_candidates.

EvaluatorTests also keeps a candidate-mutation law that was first removed on the argument that it could never fail. That argument was wrong, and the counter-example is now a test: decode is only required to return an equal value, so a registered codec that hands back the instance it encoded gives the evaluator the caller's own object to edit. The root cause is closed at the codec end too, by ArtifactCodecTests.mutable_values. That fixture has no default — () is a positive claim of immutability, the same shape as rejected_values — because an opt-in law still certifies a codec whose author never considered aliasing. It cannot simply apply to every value: requiring decode(encode(v)) is not v unconditionally would fail the built-in python-value codec on interned small integers, where sharing is harmless. The subclass declares its mutable values outright; the evaluator's mutation law observes through the kernel content digest and needs no shared helper.

The *_teeth test modules point a suite at a deliberately broken component and check its complaint, so a suite that stopped asserting would itself fail. They cover codecs, evaluators, search programs, context policies, workspaces, sandboxes, mutation surfaces, and — through broken reference callables such as a works-once proposer — the two proposer suites. They also pin the weaknesses review found: a workspace provider that leaks only when two workspaces are live, an evaluator whose drift hides in its uncertainty or evidence rather than its metrics, a sandbox that snapshots the environment in its constructor, a mutation surface that ignores the value it was asked to apply, a field that forges its own projection through __deepcopy__, a policy identity declared only for the kernel's read, a hidden random stream drawn only by the executed instance, an encode that special-cases the objects being watched, a value type whose __eq__ certifies a payload collapse, a sandbox that fabricates process results without executing, sandboxes that ignore timeout or either output limit, a sandbox that claims kernel-owned evaluation/trial/token usage, a random stream declared one decision late, a proposer that only works on its first call, a capture that re-reads only the paths it materialized, and a workspace backed by external symlinks.

tests/ subclasses the published classes for every built-in codec, all four mutation surfaces, every shipped search program, both workspace and sandbox providers, every selecting context policy, and — via the reference callables recorded above — both proposer suites, so those suites and the kernel's own conformance are the same code and cannot drift. pytest is imported by that subpackage and nowhere else in the package, pinned by an AST scan plus a subprocess check that importing meta_evolve never loads it, and surfaced as the package's one optional extra, conformance.

The codec suite checks round trips, rejection signaling, identity independence, repeated calls within one process, and common open/socket entry points. The last two are deliberately scoped evidence: they do not prove arbitrary purity or cross-process reproducibility. A separate built-in test creates artifacts in fresh interpreters under two fixed PYTHONHASHSEED values and compares their content digests.

The tutorial is executed, not illustrated. docs/adding-an-artifact-domain.md is written as one script split across fenced python blocks, followed by a single fenced text block holding the output it claims. tests/test_add_a_domain_tutorial.py joins the code back together, runs it in a fresh interpreter from an empty directory with no PYTHONPATH, and compares stdout byte for byte; it also checks that the script imports nothing but the meta_evolve root and the standard library, that every repository path the page links to exists, and that the page's "six built-in keys" claim still matches BUILTIN_CODECS. The tutorial's own codec then runs the published ArtifactCodecTests, which is the step the page tells its reader to take. Extraction beat mirroring the code into a test: a mirror drifts silently in exactly the direction that matters, because nothing forces the copy a reader sees to be the copy that ran.

docs.title: Milestone 8: harness evolution
docs.text:
Status: Shipped (closed August 14, 2026; #8). M8.1–M8.5 and #124 are implemented. M8.6 closure evidence is retained in closed, unmerged PR #162; no additional harness code or broader live-validation claim merged to main.

The canonical deterministic implementation is examples/research/harness_evolution/. M9 uses the policy_evolution example independently of the retained M8.6 closure evidence.

The whole constructible family lives under meta_evolve.harness. The built-in codec owns agent-harness / harness-manifest-v1; the schema-v1 artifact has exactly planner: TextParam and context_policy: PolicyParam. Both implement the published MutationSurfaceTests contract.

ArtifactCodec.validate_successor is optional and discovered structurally by CodecIndex. Proposal completion invokes it after encode and before creating an Artifact. The hook sees parent and candidate frozen payloads and returns a typed failure or None; codecs without it are unchanged. This is the one generic seam, and no coordinator module imports a concrete harness type.

RepositoryEpisode and EpisodeSuite are portable namespaced values.
