  → validate its committed event prefix
  → reconstruct the last complete logical state
  → rebuild verified components
  → continue only the missing authorized work
  → reach the same final event stream as uninterrupted execution

The guarantee depends on deterministic, retry-safe components and atomic commits. A live, non-reconstructable callback cannot honestly provide it.

docs.title: The running problem
docs.text:
The example climbs from 0 to target 6 by proposing parent + 1:

def propose(parent, context):
    return parent + 1

def evaluate(candidate):
    return -abs(candidate - 6)

Reaching 6 requires six successor trials and seven evaluations including the seed. The task permits eight evaluations and Greedy permits eight successor trials, leaving slack so the run stops because it satisfies the objective rather than because budget expires.

docs.title: Why ordinary local callables are insufficient
docs.text:
An in-memory function object cannot be reconstructed after the Python process dies. Durable mode therefore requires registered module-level components:

registry = meta.Registry()
proposer_ref = registry.register_proposer(
    "example:propose", "1", propose,
    deterministic=True,
    retry_safe=True,
)
evaluator_ref = registry.register_evaluator(
    "example:evaluate", "1", evaluate,
    deterministic=True,
    retry_safe=True,
    configuration={"target": 6},
)

The durable event stream records typed component references and manifests. On resume, the supplied registry must resolve compatible implementations whose source and configuration match those manifests.

The target belongs in evaluator configuration because changing it changes behavior even if the Python function name remains the same.

docs.title: Starting a durable run
docs.text:
experiment = meta.Experiment(
    task=build_task(evaluator_ref),
    seed=0,
    proposer=proposer_ref,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=8),
    registry=registry,
)
result = meta.run(
    experiment, storage=meta.Storage.durable(path), mode="durable-local"
)

Run identity derives from the declarations, not from the storage directory. Starting the same task, seed, component references, policy, and budgets on two paths produces the same run ID.

docs.title: Atomic batch commits
docs.text:
The coordinator groups each state transition into an all-or-none storage commit. A simplified run looks like:

batch 1  run + seed records
batch 2  search decision
batch 3  proposal/trial outcome
batch 4  evaluation
batch 5  next decision
...

If power fails between batches, every earlier batch is durable and the next is absent. If it fails while a batch is being written, the storage transaction commits all of it or none of it. Recovery never has to interpret half an evaluation.

The notebook's CrashAfter wrapper is only a deterministic test instrument. It permits the first n real commits and raises before the next. Production users do not install it or touch the internal commit strategy; real operating system or hardware failure supplies the interruption.

docs.title: The three recovery frontiers
docs.text:
Replay classifies the committed prefix:

Frontier Last durable fact What resume does next DECISION_READY Previous work complete Ask search for the next decision TRIAL_DECIDED Trial authorization committed Run the authorized proposer work EVALUATION_PENDING Candidate outcome committed Evaluate that committed artifact

These states prevent duplicate work. For example, a committed candidate with no evaluation is evaluated; the proposer is not called again to create a possibly different candidate.

Pull experience operations add a related boundary: an attempted but unresolved read is rolled forward using the same committed operation ID.

The sweep classifies every interior boundary:

phases = {}
total_a = boundaries + 1
for k in range(1, total_a):
    p = adir / f'phase{k}'
    s = meta.Storage.durable(p)  # install + run on one handle (see sweep note)
    install_crash(s, n=k)
    try:
        main.start_run(s, main.build_components())
    except CRASH:
        pass
    events = meta.Storage.durable(p).events.read(rid_a)
    phase = classify_frontier(events, replay_run_projection(rid_a, events)).name
    phases.setdefault(phase, []).append(k)
for name, ks in phases.items():
    print(f'  {name:<18} at boundaries {ks}')
Output
  DECISION_READY     at boundaries [1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22]
  TRIAL_DECIDED      at boundaries [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20]
  EVALUATION_PENDING at boundaries [3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21]

docs.title: The demonstrated lifecycle
docs.text:
The uninterrupted reference reaches best 6 in 49 events over 23 committed batches. Then the notebook interrupts the same logical run shape:

crash_after = max(1, committed_batches // 2)
assert 1 <= crash_after < committed_batches
path_b = tmp / 'path-B'
crash_storage = meta.Storage.durable(path_b)
crasher = install_crash(crash_storage, n=crash_after)
crashed = False
try:
    main.start_run(crash_storage, components)
except SimulatedCrash as e:
    crashed = True
    print('crashed:', e)
assert crashed and crasher.commits == crash_after
crashed_len = len(meta.Storage.durable(path_b).events.read(run_id))
print(f'events on disk  : {crashed_len}  (a genuine PARTIAL stream vs {complete_len} complete)')
Output
crashed: simulated process crash after 11 committed steps
events on disk  : 25  (a genuine PARTIAL stream vs 49 complete)

After meta.resume(...) fills the missing work, compare the interrupted and uninterrupted outcomes:

assert resumed.id == run_id
assert resumed_best == reference_best
ok = resumed_best == reference_best
print(f'interrupted == uninterrupted: {ok}  ({resumed_best} == {reference_best})')
print(f'partial stream {crashed_len} events -> recovered {resumed_len} events -> best {resumed_best}')
Output
interrupted == uninterrupted: True  (6 == 6)
partial stream 25 events -> recovered 49 events -> best 6

The advanced sweep repeats this after all 22 interior boundaries. Separate sweeps cover pushed context and pull experience:

_, _, eb, eok, ebest, rollfwd = sweep(advanced.experience_run, advanced.build_components, Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()))
print(f'experience run: {eb} boundaries, all equivalent = {eok}, best = {ebest}')
print(f'  mid-operation crash boundaries rolled forward on resume: {rollfwd}')
Output
experience run: 43 boundaries, all equivalent = True, best = 6
  mid-operation crash boundaries rolled forward on resume: 7

docs.title: Reopen is not resume
docs.text:
These operations answer different questions:

cold = meta.Run(rid_a, meta.Storage.durable(adir / 'ref'))
print('best() from a cold store :', cold.best().value)
print('winning lineage steps    :', [t.logical_step for t in cold.lineage()])
Output
best() from a cold store : 6
winning lineage steps    : [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

Run(...) rebuilds a read-only result from committed facts. It performs no new work and can inspect a completed or partial history where queries are defined.

continued = meta.resume(
    run_id,
    storage=reopened_storage,
    registry=registry,
)

resume may invoke search, proposer, and evaluator to finish missing work. It therefore requires reconstruction authority and verified components.

Resuming an already completed run is a no-op. Concurrent resume attempts use optimistic append control: one commits, while a stale writer receives EventStreamConflict rather than duplicating a transition.

docs.title: What cannot resume
docs.text:
A run may retain durable history without being resumable. Local patch callbacks, command evaluator objects, provider sessions, or closures can be inspectable after reopening while lacking a portable reconstruction contract.

Meta-Evolve raises CapabilityError instead of silently substituting a different component. Durable storage is evidence retention; resumability is an additional capability.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• The event log is append-only; crash simulation never truncates it.
  • Atomicity prevents partial logical batches.
  • Replay determines exactly which work is missing.
  • Component manifests protect behavior across process restart.
  • Run identity is logical and independent of the storage path.
  • Resume does not mean arbitrary live-model output becomes reproducible.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a committed candidate with no evaluation not run its proposer again?
  2. Why must the evaluator's target be in its manifest configuration?
  3. What is the difference between reopening and resuming?
  4. Can a non-deterministic remote provider promise a byte-identical resumed result merely because events are durable?
Answers 1. The proposal result already exists; rerunning could create a second outcome for one authorized trial. Resume continues at `EVALUATION_PENDING`. 2. The target changes scoring behavior while the function's name and source may stay constant. 3. Reopen reads committed history; resume is authorized to reconstruct components and continue missing work. 4. No. Durable observations can be retained, but equivalent future provider output requires stronger provider-specific guarantees.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Move the simulated crash from batch 11 to batch 12.

Predict which frontier the new prefix reaches, whether the event count grows, and which operation resume performs first. The final best and complete event stream must remain identical to the reference.

Next: evolve immutable source with an external grader.

docs.title: Evolve immutable source with an external grader
docs.text:
Status: Shipped.

So far, artifacts were small Python values. This chapter follows the same declarative loop when the artifact is a directory of source files and the evaluator is a real subprocess outside candidate authority.

Open the canonical executed notebook only if you want to execute the cells; this page explains the full lifecycle.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
The complete repair is:

load immutable UTF-8 source
  → propose one exact file replacement in a private workspace
  → capture a new immutable SourceTree
  → materialize it in a fresh evaluation workspace
  → run an external grader under a declared process protocol
  → commit score, evidence, usage, and parent lineage

The original checkout is never modified. A candidate proposal cannot include grader edits because the grader is not part of the candidate artifact. Runtime host isolation is a separate concern explained below.

docs.title: The broken program
docs.text:
The candidate tree contains one file, clamp.py. Its documented job is to keep value between low and high. The seed implementation is wrong; the desired replacement is:

def clamp(value, low, high):
    return max(low, min(value, high))

The evaluator-owned tests include values below, inside, and above the interval. The seed scores 0; the repaired successor scores 1.

docs.title: Step 1: load an immutable SourceTree
docs.text:
source = meta.load_source_tree(staged)
print("loaded immutable source:", tuple(source) == ("clamp.py",))
Output
loaded immutable source: True

The loader recursively captures exact relative paths and UTF-8 text. It rejects:

  • symlinks;
  • binary or non-UTF-8 content;
  • non-regular files;
  • unsafe or ambiguous paths.

There are deliberately no ignore rules. A generated __pycache__ changes the directory being declared and is rejected rather than silently omitted. Stage only intended files into a clean directory when tools may have left debris.

SourceTree is immutable. A successor is new content with parent lineage, not an in-place edit of source.

docs.title: Step 2: describe one exact patch
docs.text:
def repair(tree, context):
    return meta.TextPatch(
        path="clamp.py",
        expected=tree["clamp.py"],
        replacement=FIXED,
    )

expected is optimistic concurrency for file content. The patch applies only if the private workspace still contains the exact parent text the proposer saw. This prevents a stale patch from overwriting an unexpected revision.

PatchProposer owns the workspace lifecycle:

materialize parent → invoke patch callback → validate path/expected/replacement
→ apply exact edit → capture SourceTree → dispose workspace

Invalid path, conflict, unchanged replacement, malformed patch, and cleanup failure remain typed proposal outcomes. They are not low task scores.

docs.title: Step 3: keep the grader external
docs.text:
The evaluator declaration is:

evaluator = meta.CommandEvaluator(
    command=meta.ProcessSpec(
        argv=(python, "run_grader.py", "grader.py"),
        environment={"PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE": "1"},
    ),
    environment=meta.EvaluationEnvironment(
        name="python-clamp-tests",
        version="1",
    ),
)

For each candidate, CommandEvaluator creates a fresh workspace, materializes only the candidate source, runs the fixed command, captures bounded output, and disposes the workspace.

grader.py and run_grader.py live outside the SourceTree. The candidate cannot propose changes to them because they are not in its artifact or proposal workspace.

docs.title: The exit protocol
docs.text:
The fixed runner translates process behavior into domain outcomes:

Exit Meaning Outcome Rankable? 0 Candidate passes score=1 Yes 1 Candidate fails tests or cannot load score=0 Yes Other Grader/protocol broke EvaluatorFailure No Timeout Process exceeded wall limit TimeoutFailure No

Candidate syntax error is rankable failure because the task is to supply working source. Missing grader is not candidate performance; scoring it 0 would reward infrastructure reliability as though it measured code quality.

fault = broken_evaluator(source)
process = next(item for item in fault.evidence if item.kind == "process-result")
print("grader fault:", type(fault.failure).__name__)
print("grader fault rankable:", bool(fault.metrics))
print("grader fault process exit:", process.data["exit_code"])
print("grader fault evidence kinds:", [item.kind for item in fault.evidence])
Output
grader fault: EvaluatorFailure
grader fault rankable: False
grader fault process exit: 2
grader fault evidence kinds: ['evaluation-environment', 'process-result']

docs.title: Step 4: budget seed and successor
docs.text:
budget = meta.Budget(evaluations=2, trials=1)
task = meta.Task(
    evaluator=evaluator,
    artifact=meta.SourceTree,
    budget=budget,
)

Two evaluations cover the broken seed and one proposed successor. One trial authorizes the patch. The task owns this coordinator ceiling.

docs.title: Step 5: run the ordinary loop
docs.text:
experiment = meta.Experiment(
    task=task,
    seed=source,
    proposer=meta.PatchProposer(repair),
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=1),
)
result = meta.run(experiment, storage=storage, mode="local")

No coordinator branch knows this is Python repair. The artifact codec handles SourceTree; the proposer handles patches; the evaluator handles process execution; Greedy sees only rankable outcomes.

docs.title: Step 6: read immutable evidence
docs.text:
The saved run prints the evaluator-owned evidence and causal result:

print("source digests:", digests)
print("scores:", scores)
print("process exits:", exits)
print("failures:", failures)
print("evidence kinds:", kinds)
print("repaired best:", best.value["clamp.py"] == FIXED)
print("parent unchanged:", source["clamp.py"] != FIXED)
print("lineage length:", len(lineage))
Output
source digests: ['659bfe4a9f389018a5059f9045d6db37592c017591629d6baf5a7ab52792ca53', '08abe248cf356c0ee0322aa9329598221640460d6cf0202228097d7f4c4c21c0']
scores: [0.0, 1.0]
process exits: [1, 0]
failures: [None, None]
evidence kinds: [['evaluation-environment', 'process-result'], ['evaluation-environment', 'process-result']]
repaired best: True
parent unchanged: True
lineage length: 2

Each lineage entry includes a content digest. The repaired tree has a different digest and names the seed artifact as its parent. Reopening durable storage can read the same best artifact and lineage without touching the checkout.

Process wall time is occurrence evidence, not deterministic identity. Content, declarations, scores, and semantic outcome are the stable parts of this local example.

docs.title: Durable history is not cold resume
docs.text:
The run uses durable storage but mode="local". Its live patch callback, command evaluator, and workspace providers have no portable reconstruction manifest. Therefore:

with meta.Storage.durable(history) as reopened:
    durable = meta.Run(result.id, reopened)
    print("reopened best:", durable.best() == best)
    print("reopened lineage:", durable.lineage() == lineage)
    try:
        meta.resume(result.id, storage=reopened, registry=meta.Registry())
    except meta.CapabilityError as error:
        if "not resumable" not in str(error):
            raise
        print("cold resume: CapabilityError (local run is not resumable)")
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("local workspace run unexpectedly resumed")
Output
reopened best: True
reopened lineage: True
cold resume: CapabilityError (local run is not resumable)

Failing closed is important. Substituting a different grader or patcher after a restart would create one run ID with two behaviors.

docs.title: The subprocess boundary is not hostile isolation
docs.text:
DevelopmentSubprocessSandbox controls working directory, environment, timeout, process-group termination, and retained stdout/stderr. It does not isolate network, CPU, memory, syscalls, or arbitrary host filesystem access.

Use a hardened container or other isolation provider for untrusted code. Do not describe this development boundary as a security sandbox.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• Candidate authority is exactly the files inside the immutable tree.
  • Exact patches prevent stale overwrite and preserve the parent.
  • Proposal and evaluation use separate fresh workspaces.
  • The external grader remains outside candidate lineage.
  • Candidate-caused failure is rankable; evaluator failure is not.
  • Durable inspection does not imply resumable execution.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why include expected text in a patch?
  2. Why is a candidate syntax error score 0 while a missing grader has no metric?
  3. Does SourceTree prevent candidate code from accessing the host at runtime?
  4. Why can the run reopen but not resume?
Answers 1. It ensures the patch applies to the exact parent revision the proposer saw. 2. Syntax validity is task performance; missing evaluator infrastructure means the task was never measured. 3. No. It bounds the versioned artifact and workspace capture, not hostile-code runtime authority. 4. Stored artifacts/events are portable, but the local live callbacks and providers are not reconstructable from a registry manifest.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change the replacement to invalid Python.

Predict: the patch itself is structurally valid and commits a new source tree; the external runner exits 1; evaluation returns rankable score=0; Greedy keeps the original seed as best; the failed candidate and its process evidence remain in run.trials() but not in the winning lineage.

You now have the complete basic path: declare a task, choose search, compare it fairly, reuse experience causally, recover durable work, and evolve real source under an external evaluator.

docs.title: Feedback Descent: improve a prompt from textual feedback
docs.text:
Status: Experimental/live-only.

Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. This chapter contains the full explanation; the notebook is not required.

docs.title: The concrete problem
docs.text:
Who holds the all-time record at the Grammys for the most wins in the album of the year category?

The solver receives this question and a noisy document bundle. It does not receive the evaluator's answer, gold URL, gold-document label, or the fact that this is the Feedback Descent development row.

Two prompt candidates start from the same evidence:

candidate A
Answer the question from the supplied documents. Return only the answer.

candidate B
Find the document that directly resolves the question, ignore conflicting
distractors, and return only the answer.

The artifact being improved is the prompt itself, represented as meta.Text. The question, documents, exact-answer grader, and budget remain fixed.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Ordinary optimization says only “A scored 0 and B scored 1.” Feedback Descent adds an inspectable explanation of why one candidate is preferred, then asks an editor to derive a successor from that explanation.

prompt A ──► answer A ──┐
                         ├─► pairwise preference + textual feedback
prompt B ──► answer B ──┘                 │
                                           ▼
                              edit preferred prompt
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                  evaluate edited prompt

This lab isolates that mechanism. It does not implement the paper's full search strategy or claim to reproduce its results.

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
Feedback Descent sounds specialized, but the teaching loop is assembled from ordinary evaluated-improvement roles:

Role Concrete component Why it is separate Mutable artifact Two seed meta.Text prompts, then one edited prompt The thing being optimized is explicit and immutable Task input Candidate-visible case.md Every solver receives the same question and noisy documents Proposal evidence Structured preference plus textual feedback The edit can name exactly what observation caused it Proposer Editor session constrained by EDIT_SCHEMA It may rewrite a prompt but cannot score it Evaluator Pairwise comparison session plus local exact grading Hidden answer and ranking stay outside prompt authority Search shape Compare two seeds, edit the preferred one once This is a fixed teaching schedule, not an unbounded optimizer Budget Five individually bounded sessions One bad step cannot trigger retries until improvement appears

There is no numeric gradient. “Descent” means turning an evaluator's natural language diagnosis into the direction of the next artifact change:

observed answer difference
  → evaluator says which behavior was better and why
  → editor converts that reason into a general prompt instruction
  → unchanged task measures the successor

The algorithm is simple because Meta-Evolve already supplies immutable text, bounded provider sessions, structured evidence, typed failures, usage, and identity. The lab only has to specify who sees which files and how those five sessions connect.

docs.title: How the implementation moves data
docs.text:
run() loads one full EvaluatorCase, but immediately renders only case.public for solver workspaces. _solve() combines one prompt with that public file and asks for the closed ANSWER_SCHEMA.

PROMPTS[name] + public case
  ── _solve ──► SessionRecord(answer or failure)
  ── grade_record(expected answer, evaluator side) ──► Measurement

Only _comparison_request() receives case.answer. It writes a private comparison.md containing the reference and both observed answers, then asks for COMPARISON_SCHEMA. That response is evaluator evidence, not a prompt artifact.

The editor gets a new SourceTree with exactly:

prompt.md    preferred seed prompt
feedback.md  comparator's textual feedback

It cannot recover the hidden answer from those files. After schema validation, the code lifts value["prompt"] into a new meta.Text, rejects an empty or unchanged edit, records edit_derived_from="feedback.comparison", and calls the same _solve() and grade_record() path used for the seeds.

This reuse is what makes the final comparison interpretable: the artifact is different, while public case, model, schema, grader, and bounds remain fixed.

docs.title: Walkthrough: one improvement cycle in four phases
docs.text:
This walkthrough uses phase for an outer algorithm step. The five provider sessions inside the phases are five independent inner meta.run calls with Greedy(max_trials=1); they are not five search iterations.

Phase Meta-Evolve components State entering the phase State leaving the phase 1. Measure seeds Two immutable meta.Text artifacts; two solver SessionRequests; evaluator-owned grade_record() Prompt A, prompt B, and the same public case Two SessionRecords and two exact measurements 2. Derive feedback Comparator request with COMPARISON_SCHEMA Both observed answers plus the evaluator-only reference Preferred seed name and textual feedback, or a typed failure 3. Propose successor Editor request over a two-file SourceTree Preferred prompt.md and feedback.md; no hidden answer New meta.Text prompt with lineage to feedback.comparison 4. Measure and retain Reused solver path and exact grader; LabResult Successor prompt and the unchanged public case Edited measurement, all session evidence, artifacts, lineage, and usage

The authority boundary stays visible at every handoff. Solvers can answer but cannot grade; the comparator can read the reference but cannot edit the artifact; the editor can edit but sees only feedback; and outer Python decides whether a structured result is a measurement, a successor, or an unrankable failure.

For a concrete state trace, suppose candidate B is preferred. No live outcome is being claimed here—the names show how records would flow:

meta.Text(prompt B)
  + SessionRecord(candidate B answer)
  + SessionRecord(comparison feedback)
  ── editor request ──► meta.Text(edited prompt)
  ── unchanged solver/evaluator ──► Measurement(edited)
  ── retain ──► LabResult

docs.title: The five sessions
docs.text:
# Session Observes Produces 1 candidate_a solver Prompt A, public question and documents Structured answer A 2 candidate_b solver Prompt B, identical public question and documents Structured answer B 3 Pairwise evaluator Both answers and evaluator-only reference answer Preferred candidate and textual feedback 4 Prompt editor Preferred prompt and textual feedback only Rewritten prompt 5 Edited-prompt solver Rewritten prompt, original public question and documents Structured answer for exact grading

The editor never sees the reference answer or gold URL. Its input is exactly the preferred prompt plus the feedback, so the successor can record:

edited prompt derived_from feedback.comparison

If the comparison or editor fails, later dependent sessions do not run. Five is the ceiling for one complete path, not a promise to spend five calls after a typed failure makes the remaining comparison meaningless.

docs.title: Structured evidence
docs.text:
The evaluator must return this closed-world shape:

{
  "preferred_candidate": "candidate_a",
  "textual_feedback": "A general explanation of what the prompt should change."
}

preferred_candidate may be only candidate_a or candidate_b. Feedback must be non-empty, and extra fields are rejected. The independent validator runs for both live wrapper output and injected test output.

The editor separately returns:

{"prompt": "The complete rewritten solver prompt."}

An empty or unchanged prompt is a typed ProposerFailure; it is not evaluated as if it were a new candidate.

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:
The real implementation is deliberately small:

from sealqa_labs import UserSdkSessionRunner
from sealqa_labs.feedback_descent import run

result = run(UserSdkSessionRunner(agent_factory=build_agent))

print("preferred:", result.artifacts.get("preferred"))
print("feedback:", result.artifacts.get("feedback"))
print("edited:", result.artifacts.get("edited"))
print("derived from:", result.artifacts.get("edit_derived_from"))
print("edited measurement:", result.measurements.get("edited"))
print("usage:", result.usage)
Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
preferred: <candidate_a-or-candidate_b>
feedback: <structured evaluator rationale>
edited: <complete rewritten prompt>
derived from: feedback.comparison
edited measurement: <exact metric or typed failure>
usage: <aggregated provider usage>

Run it from a user-owned driver after authenticating your SDK:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_SDK=1 uv run python your_sealqa_driver.py feedback_descent

The five sessions all use the pinned Haiku model, equal 50-turn ceilings, a 1,800-second adapter timeout, and a 1,860-second inner wall budget.

docs.title: How to read the result
docs.text:
Inspect these fields in order:

  1. sessions: did every requested session succeed, and what did it cost?
  2. measurements.candidate_a and candidate_b: were the initial answers exact?
  3. artifacts.preferred: which prompt did the evaluator select?
  4. artifacts.feedback: is the explanation general, actionable, and grounded in the observed difference?
  5. artifacts.edited: did the editor actually change the prompt?
  6. artifacts.edit_derived_from: does lineage name the comparison evidence?
  7. measurements.edited: did the one edited evaluation improve, tie, or regress?

Possible outcomes are intentionally broader than “success”:

Outcome Honest interpretation Edited score improves The edit helped this one development case. Tie Feedback and editing bought no measured gain here. Regression The edit damaged this case; preserve the negative result. Comparison invalid There is no preference to rank or edit from. Editor unchanged No successor exists. Provider/timeout failure The attempt is unrankable, not a zero score.

One development row cannot establish general prompt quality. A robust claim would require a separately declared held-out suite and repeated compatible comparisons.

docs.title: Leakage and validity checklist
docs.text:
• Only the pairwise evaluator may read the hidden reference answer.
  • Neither solver request contains source URLs, split roles, or gold labels.
  • The editor workspace contains only prompt.md and feedback.md.
  • The edited solver sees the same public case as both initial solvers.
  • All solver arms use the same model and resource declarations.
  • A favorable edit is reported once; it is not selected from repeated reruns.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Remove “ignore conflicting distractors” from candidate B. Before running, predict:

  1. which prompt the evaluator will prefer;
  2. what general feedback it will produce;
  3. whether the edited prompt will improve, tie, regress, or fail;
  4. which evidence and lineage fields should stay unchanged.

The interesting result is not merely the final score. It is whether the recorded feedback caused an inspectable prompt change under a valid comparison.

docs.title: AutoData: improve a generation recipe with solver behavior
docs.text:
Status: Experimental/live-only.

Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. Everything needed to understand the lab is explained below.

docs.title: The concrete problem
docs.text:
What is the current age of the oldest person to sail solo across the Pacific Ocean?

This frozen row supplies the grounding documents from which a generator creates one new question-answer item. The artifact being improved is not the answer and not the generated row; it is the meta.Text generation recipe.

The seed recipe says:

Generate one unambiguous fact-seeking question answerable from the evidence.
Return its exact short answer and the document IDs used.

The lab asks whether solver behavior can identify a useful generated item and provide evidence for rewriting that recipe.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
AutoData-style generation uses downstream behavior as a quality signal:

recipe ──► generated QA item
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
 restricted solver      informed solver
 question only          question + evidence
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ▼
       deterministic acceptance checks
                    │
                    ▼
              rewrite recipe

The paper discusses weak and strong models. This lab deliberately uses the same pinned model with different context. The code roles are therefore named restricted_solver and informed_solver. Calling them weak and strong would hide the fact that context—not model capability—is the changed variable. That setup is a teaching simplification and a confounder.

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
The important move is to optimize the recipe, not to keep whichever single question looks nice. Each component has one authority:

Role Concrete component What it contributes Mutable artifact meta.Text recipe A versioned instruction that can have a successor Generator Schema-constrained session Applies a recipe to public evidence and proposes one QA item Restricted probe Same model with question.md only Tests whether evidence is unnecessary or the answer leaks Informed probe Same model with selected evidence.md Tests whether cited evidence supports recovery Evaluator quality_checks() in local Python Converts observations into explicit acceptance reasons Proposer Recipe-rewriter session Turns the report into a generalized successor recipe Search shape Seed evaluation → one rewrite → successor evaluation Makes the causal comparison small and inspectable

The generated QA item is an evaluation episode, not the durable thing being optimized. A seed recipe and successor recipe may each generate different questions; comparison asks whether the recipe produces an item that passes the same quality protocol.

recipe artifact
  → generator applies it
  → two controlled solver contexts probe the item
  → deterministic evaluator produces accepted + reasons
  → rewriter uses that evidence to propose the next recipe artifact

This is why the method is easy to build with Meta-Evolve: artifact lineage, bounded sessions, evidence, schema failure, and usage already exist. AutoData's domain logic is the small quality_checks() function and the choice of what the two solver arms may see.

docs.title: How _evaluate_recipe() assembles one evaluation
docs.text:
The function first writes the public SealQA bundle to evidence.md and asks the generator for ITEM_SCHEMA. If generation fails validation, it returns one session plus a rejection report and spends no solver calls.

For a valid item it builds two fresh workspaces:

restricted_solver/
  question.md

informed_solver/
  question.md
  evidence.md   only documents named by evidence_doc_ids

The code resolves local document IDs against the available public bundle. An unknown ID therefore cannot smuggle in external evidence; it becomes the deterministic unknown_evidence_document reason.

Both _solver() calls use the same answer instructions, ANSWER_SCHEMA, SDK wrapper declaration, limits, and wall budget. Only the informed workspace has evidence. quality_checks() then reads the generator item and both SessionRecords. It never calls a model:

schema valid?
IDs known?
answer text absent from question?
both solver sessions healthy?
restricted answer differs from reference?
informed answer exactly matches reference?

The complete dictionary—generated item, solver outputs, accepted, and every reason—is written into LabResult.artifacts["evidence"]. The rewrite workspace contains the seed recipe and this report. The successor is lifted back into meta.Text and sent through the identical _evaluate_recipe() function.

docs.title: Walkthrough: one improvement cycle in three phases
docs.text:
Each phase below is outer Python orchestration. Its generator, solver, and rewriter sessions are separate inner meta.run calls with one trial each; the lab does not run three greedy search iterations.

Phase Meta-Evolve components What the candidate can observe Evaluator-owned result 1. Evaluate seed recipe Seed meta.Text; generator request; restricted and informed solver requests Generator sees the public bundle; restricted solver sees only the generated question; informed solver sees only selected evidence quality_checks() records accepted/rejected reasons and a seed measurement 2. Propose successor recipe Rewriter request; successor meta.Text Seed recipe, generated item, solver records, and the complete deterministic report Schema and non-identity checks decide whether a successor exists 3. Evaluate and retain successor The same _evaluate_recipe() protocol; LabResult A fresh generator applies only the successor recipe; solver visibility remains split Successor acceptance measurement plus both recipes, reports, sessions, lineage, and usage

The state transition is therefore:

meta.Text(seed recipe)
  ── generator + two probes ──► seed acceptance report
  ── rewriter SessionRequest ──► meta.Text(successor recipe)
  ── same generator + two probes ──► successor acceptance report
  ── retain ──► LabResult

The generated QA items are temporary evaluation episodes. They appear in the evidence record, but the lineage edge connects recipe to recipe. The local acceptance gate, not the generator or rewriter, decides whether each episode meets the declared behavior.

docs.title: The seven sessions
docs.text:
One recipe evaluation uses three SDK sessions:

  1. generate a structured QA item from the frozen document bundle;
  2. ask the restricted solver with no documents;
  3. ask the informed solver with the generated item's selected documents.

The complete path is:

# Session Purpose 1 Seed generator Apply the seed recipe. 2 Seed restricted solver Test whether the question leaks or is already known. 3 Seed informed solver Test whether selected evidence supports the reference answer. 4 Recipe rewriter Generalize from the seed acceptance report. 5 Successor generator Apply the rewritten recipe. 6 Successor restricted solver Repeat the restricted check. 7 Successor informed solver Repeat the grounded check.

The local checks between sessions are deterministic and make no provider calls:

3 seed sessions + 1 rewrite + 3 successor sessions = 7 maximum

docs.title: The generated-item contract
docs.text:
The generator must return:

{
  "question": "One generated fact-seeking question",
  "reference_answer": "One exact short answer",
  "evidence_doc_ids": ["doc-03", "doc-09"]
}

The schema requires all three fields, non-empty strings, and no extra fields. Document IDs must exist in the candidate-visible bundle. They are stable local IDs—not upstream URLs or labels that reveal which source is gold.

The reference_answer here belongs to the synthetic item produced by the generator. It is not the evaluator-only answer of the frozen SealQA row.

docs.title: Deterministic quality checks
docs.text:
An item is accepted only when every check passes:

Check Rejection reason Meaning Schema structured-output failure Required fields are missing or malformed. Evidence IDs unknown_evidence_document The recipe cited a document it never received. Leakage reference_answer_leaked_in_question The question gives away its own answer. Restricted exact answer restricted_solver_already_knows_answer The item may be trivial, memorized, or leaking. Informed exact answer informed_solver_cannot_recover_answer Selected evidence does not establish the answer. Session health solver_failure At least one solver produced no rankable answer.

In compact form, the desired behavior is:

restricted answer != reference answer
informed answer    == reference answer

This is a proxy for grounded usefulness, not proof. The restricted model may guess incorrectly despite already knowing the fact, and the informed model may match for the wrong reason.

docs.title: Recipe rewriting and lineage
docs.text:
The rewriter sees:

  • the seed recipe;
  • the complete generated item;
  • both solver answers or failures;
  • the acceptance decision and rejection reasons.

It is told to generalize rather than copy the generated question or answer. Its structured output is simply:

{"recipe": "The complete successor generation recipe."}

The result retains both recipes, both generated examples, both solver pairs, both acceptance reports, evaluator identity, typed failures, and aggregate usage. That makes the causal story inspectable:

seed recipe + seed rejection evidence ──► successor recipe

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:
from sealqa_labs import UserSdkSessionRunner
from sealqa_labs.autodata import run

result = run(UserSdkSessionRunner(agent_factory=build_agent))

print("seed recipe:", result.artifacts["seed_recipe"])
print("successor recipe:", result.artifacts.get("successor_recipe"))
print("evidence:", result.artifacts["evidence"])
print("measurements:", result.measurements)
print("usage:", result.usage)
Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
seed recipe: <original generation instructions>
successor recipe: <evidence-guided rewritten instructions>
evidence: <generated items, solver answers, decisions, and rejection reasons>
measurements: <seed and successor acceptance metrics or typed failures>
usage: <aggregated provider usage>

Run it with:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_SDK=1 uv run python your_sealqa_driver.py autodata

docs.title: How to read the result
docs.text:
Compare the two acceptance reports rather than looking only at the final flag:

Seed Successor Interpretation rejected accepted The rewrite fixed the observed gate on this one attempt. rejected rejected Inspect whether the reason changed; the rewrite may still have altered behavior. accepted accepted There may have been no useful error signal for rewriting. accepted rejected The rewrite regressed the recipe. failure any The failed arm is unrankable and should not be treated as rejection.

One generated item per recipe is a mechanism demonstration. It does not estimate a stable acceptance rate, diversity, or downstream training value.

docs.title: Leakage and comparison checklist
docs.text:
• The restricted workspace contains only question.md.
  • The informed workspace adds evidence.md; model and bounds stay identical.
  • Neither solver receives the frozen row's hidden answer or URLs.
  • The generator may see public document text but no gold label.
  • The rewriter sees generated evidence, not the held-out behavior of future generated items.
  • Same-model/different-context results are not described as weak-vs-strong model evidence.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Modify the recipe to require two independent evidence document IDs. Predict:

  1. whether unknown-document rejection becomes more common;
  2. whether the informed solver becomes more reliable;
  3. whether leakage changes at all;
  4. what a rejected successor would teach you about the recipe rather than the model.

docs.title: Meta-Harness precursor: improve a bounded local harness
docs.text:
Status: Experimental/live-only.

Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. The notebook is not required to follow this chapter.

Superseded teaching precursor

This historical local lab is not the M8 API. Its claims remain scoped to the precursor that ran them. For typed harness artifacts, trusted mutation validation, portable episodes, comparison, and export, use the M8 harness guide.

docs.title: The concrete problems
docs.text:
The diagnostic row asks:

How many NBA players have scored 60 or more points in a regular season game since 2023?

The mutator may inspect the baseline's attempt on that row. It does not see the unseen validation row, whose question asks how many current and former Real Madrid players appear in the latest Forbes top-ten highest-paid-athletes list.

The experiment asks whether changing a planner and context policy after one diagnostic failure helps on that separate validation case.

docs.title: What “harness” means here
docs.text:
The local harness is an ordinary shipped meta.SourceTree containing exactly two files:

planner.md
context_policy.json

The baseline is conceptually:

planner.md
  Answer from supplied evidence. Prefer recent documents.
  Return only the short answer.

context_policy.json
  {"max_documents": 5, "order": "given"}

planner.md controls how the solver reasons and formats its reply. context_policy.json controls how many documents enter the solver workspace. The order is fixed to given in this precursor.

This is intentionally smaller than a production harness. There are no new runtime types, portable manifests, automatic replay, or promotion records.

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
This lab widens the artifact from one prompt to two coordinated files while keeping every control outside that tree:

Role Concrete component Boundary it demonstrates Mutable artifact Ordinary immutable meta.SourceTree Planner and context policy can change together Diagnostic evaluator Baseline solver plus local exact grade Produces evidence about current harness behavior Proposer Mutator session over read-only prior source/evidence Suggests file replacements but cannot apply arbitrary paths Mutation guard apply_mutation() Enforces allowlist and JSON semantics before evaluation Validation evaluator Same unseen row for baseline and candidate Measures the intended harness difference fairly Comparison compare() over two Measurements Reports improvement, tie, regression, or unrankable failure Promotion Constant False outside the candidate A better score does not deploy anything

The research algorithm is therefore only this composition:

observe baseline on development evidence
  → propose a bounded source change
  → reject changes outside authority
  → evaluate parent and successor on untouched validation
  → report comparison without promotion

Meta-Evolve already provides the versioned tree, session failures, evidence, usage, and evaluator identity. The precursor adds no coordinator behavior. Its domain code is a two-path allowlist, one JSON validator, document slicing, and an equal-arm comparison.

docs.title: How the two files affect solver execution
docs.text:
_solve() is the only function that interprets the harness. It parses context_policy.json, takes the first max_documents in fixed given order, renders them into validation.md, and uses planner.md as the solver instructions:

SourceTree.context_policy.json ──► number of visible documents
SourceTree.planner.md          ──► reasoning and answer instructions
public SolverCase             ──► validation.md

This means a mutation has two understandable levers: change how the model is instructed, change how much evidence it receives, or change both. It cannot add a tool, swap a model, reorder documents, alter the grader, or spend more sessions because none of those controls are interpreted from the artifact.

_mutation_request() materializes prior files under prior/, diagnostic measurement/answer/trace under evidence/, and the lifecycle warning under controls/. The paths are read-only evidence in the mutator's workspace. The returned files object is not trusted as a patch until apply_mutation() checks paths, UTF-8 strings, non-identity, and policy JSON.

Only after that guard returns a new immutable tree are the two validation sessions authorized. Invalid mutation therefore cannot consume held-out evaluation or leave a partial successor.

docs.title: Walkthrough: one improvement cycle in four phases
docs.text:
These are outer orchestration phases, not repeated search iterations. Each solver or mutator session is an independent, one-trial inner meta.run.

Phase Meta-Evolve components State entering the phase State leaving the phase 1. Diagnose parent Baseline SourceTree; diagnostic solver request; local exact grader Baseline planner/policy and the public diagnostic case Baseline SessionRecord, diagnostic measurement, answer, and trace kinds 2. Propose and guard mutation Mutator request; apply_mutation() authority check Read-only prior source and diagnostic evidence; no validation row Candidate SourceTree, or a typed failure with no successor 3. Validate equal arms Two solver requests using the same unseen public row Baseline and candidate trees under identical model, schema, grader, and budgets Baseline and candidate validation measurements 4. Compare and retain Evaluator-owned compare(); LabResult Both rankable measurements or a typed failure Improvement/tie/regression/failure label, artifacts, evidence, usage, and automatic_promotion=False

The bounded state transition is:

SourceTree(baseline)
  ── diagnostic evaluator ──► measurement + trace evidence
  ── mutator SessionRequest ──► proposed file replacements
  ── apply_mutation allowlist ──► SourceTree(candidate)
  ── equal unseen validation ──► comparison
  ── retain without promotion ──► LabResult

The mutation proposal is not itself an artifact. Outer Python first validates its paths and contents, then creates an immutable successor tree. This is the point where Meta-Evolve's proposal/promotion separation is concrete: the model suggests files, the experiment admits or rejects them, the evaluator compares them, and no component deploys the result.

docs.title: The four sessions
docs.text:
baseline harness ──► diagnostic attempt
       │                    │
       │                    ▼
       │            source + score + trace
       │                    │
       │                    ▼
       │              mutation session
       │                    │
       ├──────────────┐     ▼
       ▼              ▼  candidate harness
baseline validation  candidate validation
       └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                      ▼
          equal-declaration comparison
# Session Candidate-visible inputs Output 1 Baseline diagnostic Baseline harness and diagnostic public case Structured answer, trace, usage or failure 2 Harness mutator Complete prior source and diagnostic record Proposed file edits 3 Baseline validation Baseline harness and unseen public validation case Structured answer 4 Candidate validation Candidate harness and the same validation case Structured answer

The mutator's read-only workspace materializes:

  • the complete prior planner.md and context_policy.json;
  • the diagnostic exact score;
  • the baseline's candidate answer or typed failure;
  • recorded tool-trace kinds;
  • the lifecycle and authority warning.

It does not contain the validation case, evaluator answer, permission state, budget controls, audit history, or promotion decision.

docs.title: Mutation authority
docs.text:
The structured mutation shape is:

{
  "files": {
    "planner.md": "Complete replacement planner text",
    "context_policy.json": "{\"max_documents\": 10, \"order\": \"given\"}"
  }
}

The local validator applies an exact allowlist:

allowed
  planner.md
  context_policy.json

protected examples
  evaluation_data.json
  permissions.json
  budgets.json
  audit_history.jsonl
  evidence.jsonl
  promotion.json

Any path outside the two-file allowlist is a typed PolicyViolation. Protected controls are named in its evidence, and no successor SourceTree is created. Invalid UTF-8 values or malformed context-policy JSON are typed InvalidOutput. Empty or unchanged edits are typed ProposerFailure.

The policy JSON must contain a positive integer max_documents and "order": "given". This validates the candidate before any held-out provider session is spent.

docs.title: Equal validation
docs.text:
Baseline and candidate are evaluated on the same unseen row with:

  • the same declared user-owned SDK wrapper;
  • the same answer schema and normalized exact grader;
  • the same turn, timeout, and wall declarations;
  • the same public document order;
  • the same fixture-row checksum in evaluator identity.

The harness artifact is the intended difference. A comparison result is one of:

Result Meaning improvement Candidate exact score is higher. tie Both valid arms have the same exact score. regression Candidate exact score is lower. unrankable_typed_failure At least one arm produced no valid metric.

The result also states automatic_promotion = False. Search or comparison may identify a better local artifact; neither the candidate nor this evaluator may deploy it.

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:
from sealqa_labs import UserSdkSessionRunner
from sealqa_labs.meta_harness import run

result = run(UserSdkSessionRunner(agent_factory=build_agent))

print("baseline:", result.artifacts["baseline"])
print("candidate:", result.artifacts.get("candidate"))
print("comparison:", result.artifacts.get("comparison"))
print("automatic promotion:", result.artifacts.get("automatic_promotion", False))
print("measurements:", result.measurements)
print("usage:", result.usage)
Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
baseline: <planner and context-policy SourceTree>
candidate: <allowlisted successor SourceTree or None>
comparison: <improvement, tie, regression, or unrankable typed failure>
automatic promotion: False
measurements: <equal-declaration validation measurements>
usage: <aggregated provider usage>

Run it with:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_SDK=1 uv run python your_sealqa_driver.py meta_harness

If mutation is invalid, only two sessions are needed: the diagnostic and mutator. The baseline/candidate validation pair is skipped because there is no admissible successor to compare.

docs.title: How to interpret a result
docs.text:
An improvement means only that one diagnostic-informed mutation performed better on one unseen row. It does not establish that:

  • the planner change rather than the context-size change caused the gain;
  • the candidate generalizes to a broader repository task distribution;
  • the extra context is cost-effective;
  • the harness should be promoted;
  • the experiment can be durably replayed.

A tie can still reveal that the mutation changed cost, document visibility, or failure behavior without changing exact accuracy. A regression is valuable evidence that the diagnostic adaptation overfit or removed useful context.

docs.title: Authority and validity checklist
docs.text:
• Did the candidate change only the two permitted paths?
  • Was a forbidden-control proposal rejected without a successor?
  • Did the mutator see complete diagnostic evidence but no validation row?
  • Did both validation arms use identical declarations and document order?
  • Are failures reported by kind rather than converted to zero?
  • Is promotion still explicitly false?
  • Is this chapter still labeled a superseded precursor rather than current API?

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Lower max_documents from 5 to 2 without changing the planner. Before running, predict:

  1. whether the useful document remains visible;
  2. whether cost or usage should change;
  3. whether the candidate will improve, tie, regress, or fail;
  4. why even an improvement would not authorize promotion.

docs.title: EvoSkill: induce a reusable skill from recorded failures
docs.text:
Status: Experimental/live-only.

Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. This chapter is complete without it.

docs.title: The concrete problem
docs.text:
One held-out question asks:

How many airlines are members of IATA, the organization that supports airline activity and helps formulate industry policy and standards?

The skill builder never sees that row. It receives experience from two separate induction rows, then the unchanged baseline and skill-augmented agents are compared on this and one other held-out row.

The artifact being improved is a shipped meta.SkillSet: an immutable mapping from a path such as skills/sealqa.md to one inspectable Markdown document.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
An EvoSkill-style loop turns concrete agent failures into reusable procedures:

induction case 1 ──► recorded failure ──┐
                                        ├─► failure analysis ──► Markdown skill
induction case 2 ──► recorded failure ──┘                           │
                                                                    ▼
held-out case 1 ──► baseline vs skill-augmented comparison          │
held-out case 2 ──► baseline vs skill-augmented comparison ◄────────┘

This lab separates three questions that are often blurred together:

  1. Did the baseline agent fail on induction cases?
  2. Did an analyzer actually read and generalize from those failures?
  3. Did the resulting skill help unchanged agents on held-out cases?

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
EvoSkill becomes a short composition once failure collection, proposal, and held-out evaluation are kept as different components:

Role Concrete component Why it exists Episode runner _solve() using the common bounded session adapter Produces comparable answers or typed failures Evaluator Local grade_record() Keeps expected answers outside agent authority Experience Two EvidenceDraft induction records Makes prior failure observable without leaking gold answers Analyzer Pull-enabled session Chooses which prior records to inspect and generalizes patterns Proposer/builder Separate schema-constrained session Converts analysis into an inspectable skill artifact Mutable artifact Shipped immutable meta.SkillSet Versions the reusable procedure as ordinary Markdown Validation Two baseline/skill held-out pairs Tests transfer without reusing induction cases

The “algorithm” is not hidden inside one giant prompt:

run baseline episodes
  → grade externally
  → expose bounded failure evidence
  → analyze through audited experience pull
  → build a typed skill artifact
  → inject only that artifact into fresh held-out agents
  → compare each pair externally

This is simple to build because Meta-Evolve already supplies SkillSet, experience grants, derivation, session accounting, typed failure, and immutable artifacts. The lab-specific code decides what a safe failure record contains and how the Markdown is inserted into the held-out instruction block.

docs.title: How records become a skill without leaking evaluation
docs.text:
For each induction row, _solve() receives only its public case. Local grading then creates a Measurement. _failure_evidence() deliberately projects that full evaluator state into a smaller candidate-visible record:

included: case_id, prediction, exact-if-valid, failure_kind
omitted:  expected answer, URLs, gold document, held-out content

Those two records become seed_evidence in the analyzer's inner run. Because the analyzer also receives PullAccess, it must actively search/open them; the run records whether it did. ANALYSIS_SCHEMA forces separate failure_patterns and procedures, so the next step receives structured generalization rather than raw hidden evaluator state.

The builder is a new session with only analysis.json. It cannot query the induction experience or inspect held-out rows. Its validated Markdown is lifted into:

meta.SkillSet({"skills/sealqa.md": skill_markdown})

For held-out evaluation, _solve() is reused unchanged. The skill arm differs only by appending the rendered skill to BASE_INSTRUCTIONS. This makes the skill artifact—not a model, case, schema, or budget change—the intended cause of any measured difference.

docs.title: Walkthrough: one improvement cycle in four phases
docs.text:
The four phases describe the outer lab algorithm. The eight SDK sessions inside them are independent inner meta.run calls with one trial each, not eight optimizer iterations.

Phase Meta-Evolve components Candidate-visible observation Retained evaluator result 1. Record induction behavior Baseline solver requests; local grader; two EvidenceDrafts Each solver sees only its public induction case Predictions, exact-if-valid, and failure kinds; expected answers stay private 2. Analyze bounded experience Pull-enabled analyzer request with meta.PullAccess Only the two projected failure records, read through audited pull operations Failure patterns, procedures, pull counters, or a typed failure 3. Build successor skill Builder request; immutable meta.SkillSet analysis.json only; no raw experience or held-out rows One validated Markdown skill at skills/sealqa.md 4. Compare on held-out rows Four fresh solver requests; reused grader; per-row comparison; LabResult Baseline sees base instructions; skill arm adds only the rendered skill Two independent comparison labels plus sessions, measurements, lineage, experience usage, and provider usage

The artifact and evidence flow is:

baseline induction SessionRecords
  ── evaluator projection ──► two EvidenceDraft failure records
  ── PullAccess analyzer ──► structured patterns and procedures
  ── builder SessionRequest ──► SkillSet(skills/sealqa.md)
  ── two equal held-out pairs ──► two external comparisons
  ── retain ──► LabResult

There is no mutable skill before phase 3. The analyzer proposes an explanation, the builder proposes Markdown, schema checks lift that Markdown into the versioned artifact, and only fresh held-out evaluations measure it. If analysis or building fails, the lab retains the typed failure and does not spend the held-out sessions.

docs.title: The eight sessions
docs.text:
# Session Purpose 1 Induction episode 1 Run the unchanged baseline on frozen row 5. 2 Induction episode 2 Run the unchanged baseline on frozen row 6. 3 Failure analyzer Pull both recorded failure records and propose patterns/procedures. 4 Skill builder Convert the analysis into one Markdown skill with checks. 5 Held-out 1 baseline Run unchanged instructions on frozen row 7. 6 Held-out 1 skill Run identical instructions plus the skill on row 7. 7 Held-out 2 baseline Run unchanged instructions on frozen row 8. 8 Held-out 2 skill Run identical instructions plus the skill on row 8.

There is no skill evaluation on induction rows and no skill construction from held-out rows. That isolation prevents the builder from simply encoding the answers on which the skill is judged.

docs.title: What an induction failure contains
docs.text:
Each completed induction episode is graded locally. The experience record contains:

{
  "case_id": "longseal-004",
  "prediction": "the agent's answer, if any",
  "exact": 0.0,
  "failure_kind": null
}

If the provider or adapter fails, exact is absent and failure_kind names the typed outcome. The record deliberately omits:

  • the evaluator's expected answer;
  • source or gold URLs;
  • the gold-document label;
  • held-out row contents.

This makes the failure complete as an observation of what the agent did without turning evaluator secrets into proposer-visible experience.

docs.title: Shipped experience-pull seam
docs.text:
The analyzer is not handed a manually concatenated failure report. The two failure records are committed as seed evaluation evidence in an ordinary inner run, and the analyzer receives bounded meta.PullAccess:

meta.PullAccess(
    max_operations=20,
    max_results=20,
    max_records=100,
    max_chars=32_000,
)

A user-owned SDK custom tool can search and open those strictly prior records. The proposal must declare which experience it derived from. Pull usage is retained separately from provider token/wall usage.

That distinction yields two different null results:

skill did not help, analyzer used experience
skill did not help, analyzer never read the offered experience

The second says nothing about whether failure-driven induction helps; it says the configured agent did not exercise the mechanism.

docs.title: Analyzer and skill contracts
docs.text:
The analyzer returns:

{
  "failure_patterns": ["General pattern observed across failures"],
  "procedures": ["Reusable action an agent should take"]
}

The separate builder sees this analysis—not the held-out cases—and returns:

{
  "skill_markdown": "# Skill title\n\nProcedure...\n\n## Verification\n- Check..."
}

The emitted meta.SkillSet contains one path:

skills/sealqa.md

Keeping it as Markdown makes the learned procedure directly inspectable. The builder instruction requires explicit verification checks so the skill is more than generic advice such as “be careful.”

docs.title: Held-out comparison
docs.text:
For each held-out row, two fresh sessions receive the same public question, documents, model, answer schema, turn/timeout/wall bounds, and exact grader. Only the instruction block differs:

baseline arm
  base solver instructions

skill arm
  base solver instructions
  + rendered skills/sealqa.md

Each pair is classified independently:

Result Meaning improvement Skill exact score is higher. tie Both valid arms have the same score. regression Skill exact score is lower. unrankable_typed_failure At least one arm has no metric.

The report retains both results. It does not average a provider failure into a low score or hide a regression behind the other row's improvement.

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:

Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
analysis: <failure patterns and procedures>
skill set: <one inspectable Markdown skill>
experience usage: <operations, records, characters, and unused evidence>
held-out comparisons: <two improvement, tie, regression, or failure labels>

Run it with:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_SDK=1 uv run python your_sealqa_driver.py evoskill

If analysis or building fails, held-out sessions are skipped: there is no valid skill artifact to compare. Eight is the maximum complete path.

docs.title: How to interpret the result
docs.text:
Read these facts separately:

  1. Were the induction episodes valid wrong answers or typed failures?
  2. How many experience operations, records, and characters did the analyzer use?
  3. Are the reported failure patterns supported by both episodes?
  4. Does the Markdown skill contain concrete procedures and verification checks?
  5. What happened on each held-out pair—improvement, tie, regression, or failure?
  6. Did skill augmentation change provider usage as well as correctness?

Two held-out examples demonstrate the comparison mechanism; they do not support a general claim that the skill transfers across SealQA or other task families.

docs.title: Isolation and validity checklist
docs.text:
• Rows 5–6 appear only in induction and failure evidence.
  • Rows 7–8 appear only in the four held-out sessions.
  • Failure evidence omits reference answers, URLs, and split labels.
  • Analyzer and builder are separate provider sessions.
  • Pull counters show whether offered experience was actually used.
  • Baseline and skill arms otherwise share compatible declarations.
  • Ties, regressions, failures, and unused experience remain visible.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Remove the requirement for verification checks from the skill-builder instruction. Before running, predict:

  1. whether the skill becomes shorter but less actionable;
  2. whether analyzer pull usage should change;
  3. which held-out arm is most likely to tie or regress;
  4. what evidence would distinguish a bad skill from unused experience.

TARGET = 12
MOVES = (-2, 1, 5)

docs.title: Milestone 2 tour: one loop, replaceable search¶
docs.text: Milestone 2 keeps task execution fixed while making search replaceable and results fairly comparable. M2.1 introduced replayable archive decisions, linked decision explanations, and a shared policy conformance contract. M2.2 added independent BestOfN. M2.3 added a retained Population with deterministic tournament selection. M2.4 added immutable run summaries, strict comparison, and the canonical policy benchmark.

docs.title: 1. Keep the task fixed and swap only search¶
docs.text: The seed is evaluated once. max_trials counts successor proposals, while the task budget counts all evaluations including that seed.

docs.title: 2. Compare only compatible runs¶
docs.text: Run.compare() rejects mismatched evaluator/proposer declarations, objectives, budgets, or starting artifacts. Different policies, policy configurations, and root seeds are allowed. Exact score equality is a tie; usage never breaks one.

docs.title: 3. Optional kernel inspection: decisions explain themselves¶
docs.text: The public callable path ends above. The underscore projection below is an internal diagnostic used here to show the M2 record model: every policy decision has a linked explanation; Population additionally records one ArchiveUpdate for every completed evaluation.

docs.title: 4. Rebuild the same projection from retained facts¶
docs.text: M2 replay means folding the retained in-memory event tuple and reproducing historical policy decisions. It does not yet mean process restart, persistent storage, or resume; those remain later milestones.

docs.title: Where to go next¶
docs.text: Run main.py for the concise 40-seed report, then open policy_comparison.ipynb for complete distributions and representative star/chain/tree lineages. Those results are a small deterministic illustration in the locked project environment, not broad scientific evidence or a cross-version CPython guarantee. Local callable equality is declaration-based (module:qualname) and does not prove behavioral equivalence.

docs.title: Fair comparison of three search policies¶
docs.text: This canonical Milestone 2 sweep compares BestOfN, Greedy, and Population on the same target 12, moves (-2, 1, 5), initial artifact 0, primary score -abs(value - 12), nine-evaluation/eight-trial budget, and root seeds 0 through 39. Population has size 3 and tournament size 2.

docs.title: What the lineages mean¶
docs.text: BestOfN always expands zero, so [0, 5] is one spoke from a star. Its result is also a proof: independent one-step successors are limited to {-2, 1, 5}, making 5 and score -7 the best possible. Greedy's representative is the accepted chain [0, 5, 10, 11, 12]. Population creates a tree through tournament expansion and retention; [0, 5, 10, 11, 12] is the winning branch of that larger tree.

docs.title: Evidence boundary¶
docs.text: This is a small deterministic illustration in the locked project environment, not broad scientific evidence and not a cross-version CPython guarantee. The user proposer continues to use random.Random.choice through context.rng, matching the existing accepted example contract. Local callable comparison uses module:qualname declaration identity; it does not prove behavioral equivalence.

docs.title: Derivation, replay, and fair memory comparison¶
docs.text: This lab focuses on the M3.4 distinction between experience observed and experience declared as causal. It then checks that derivation survives replay and that runs with different memory strategies remain comparable.

docs.title: 1. See where reuse changes the outcome¶
docs.text: All variants spend the same task budget. Only the three memory-aware runs can turn the two failed evaluations into the successful value 10.

docs.title: 2. Inspect exact committed derivation¶
docs.text: A failed evaluation may still carry useful derivation. The second ordinary proposal cites one failure; the third cites two failures and, for pull variants, the compared trial occurrences.

docs.title: 3. Replay the same edge graph¶
docs.text: Replay validates the event stream and rebuilds derivation from durable proposals. It does not call the live context selector, reader, filtering code, or renderer.

docs.title: 4. See the serialization compatibility rule¶
docs.text: Empty derivation is omitted, so old proposal and event bytes remain unchanged. Non-empty derivation is encoded normally. An explicitly encoded empty default is rejected as non-canonical.

docs.title: 5. Compare different memory strategies fairly¶
docs.text: Memory declarations may differ. Compatibility still requires equal evaluator, proposer, objective, task/run budgets, artifact declaration, and initial digest. The comparison reports memory-declaration equality rather than rejecting the pair.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: M3.4 does not claim that every observed record caused a result. It preserves the proposer's explicit usage intent while the coordinator independently enforces visibility, ordering, budgets, failure semantics, and evaluation authority.

docs.title: Milestone 3 tour: experience that remains causal¶
docs.text:
Milestone 3 makes earlier work useful to later proposers without turning memory into ambient authority. This tour follows the four slices in order: M3.1 temporal graph, M3.2 pushed context, M3.3 audited pull access, and M3.4 declared derivation and comparison.

The deterministic experiment deliberately produces two failed evaluations. Memory-aware variants can then reuse those failures to reach 10; the no-memory variant cannot.

docs.title: 1. Run the same experiment four ways¶
docs.text: Task, seed, proposer, evaluator, chain search, random seed, and task/run budgets stay fixed. Only the memory declaration changes.

docs.title: 2. M3.1 — the temporal experience graph¶
docs.text: The graph is a read model over committed trials and records. Nodes are causal occurrences, not deduplicated payloads. An as_of boundary can reveal the past without leaking future trials.

docs.title: 3. M3.2 — policy-pushed context¶
docs.text: A context policy chooses a bounded, exact bundle before the proposer runs. The bundle stores structured records, a canonical rendering, a reason, truncation, and usage. It is replayed rather than selected again.

docs.title: 4. M3.3 — agent-directed pull access¶
docs.text: The reader lets a proposer search, open, traverse, and compare within a strictly-prior grant. Every attempt is charged and resolves to success, opaque denial, or content-free exhaustion. Usage is cumulative inside each grant.

docs.title: 5. M3.4 — declare what actually caused the proposal¶
docs.text: Observation and use are distinct. derived_from must be a unique ordered subsequence of the committed push-then-pull ledger. Valid edges survive failed evaluations and typed proposer failures; unauthorized declarations become policy failures.

docs.title: What to keep in your head¶
docs.text:
• Graph: what committed experience existed at a logical time.
  • Push: what a policy placed in front of the proposer.
  • Pull: what the proposer chose to inspect through a bounded capability.
  • Derivation: which observed references the proposer says it actually used.
  • Evaluation: still independent of proposer authority.

The example is a small deterministic illustration, not broad scientific evidence. Its purpose is to make the authority and replay contracts tangible.

docs.title: Push and pull lab: two routes to the same experience¶
docs.text:
Push and pull share committed records but express different decisions. Push records a policy's selection before execution. Pull records the proposer's own bounded investigation during execution.

This lab inspects both channels and then reconstructs the canonical observation ledger used by M3.4.

docs.title: 1. Inspect pushed bundles¶
docs.text: The demo's FailedAncestors policy pushes only failed ancestor evaluations. Notice how the number of selected failures grows as the chain advances.

docs.title: 2. Inspect pull grants and operations¶
docs.text: Each successor gets a new grant with as_of = logical_step - 1. The final proposer searches two failed evaluations, opens both, and compares their trials.

docs.title: 3. Reconstruct the push-then-pull ledger¶
docs.text: The ledger is ordered by committed observation: bundle references first, then successful pull results in operation order. References and structured record references are deduplicated by first occurrence.

docs.title: 4. Compare channel-specific usage¶
docs.text: Memory access is measured but does not consume task or run budgets. Context usage counts selected records and rendered characters. Pull usage additionally counts attempts and returned references.

docs.title: Try next¶
docs.text: Change FailedAncestors to push only one failure, lower PullAccess.max_operations, or remove the comparison call. Predict the changed ledger and usage before rerunning. The interesting question is not merely whether memory helps, but which access decision helped at what cost.

import inspect import sys from pathlib import Path import meta_evolve as meta # main.py lives next to this notebook; add its dir so its module-level # (source-digestible) proposer/evaluator/helpers can be imported. sys.path.insert(0, str(Path('examples/operations/crash_recovery').resolve())) import main # the runnable example this notebook mirrors TARGET = main.TARGET print(inspect.getsource(main.propose)) print(inspect.getsource(main.evaluate)) 
def propose(parent: object, context: object) -> object:
    """Climb toward the target by one each step. Deterministic and retry-safe:
    the same parent always yields the same child, so replaying it during
    recovery reproduces the identical candidate.

    ``context`` is deliberately ignored: this is a fixed +1 climb with no
    randomness. (Sibling example 01 instead draws from ``context.rng`` -- that
    is where the per-step context earns its keep.)"""

    return parent + 1

def evaluate(candidate: object) -> float:
    """Higher is better; the search maximizes this score. Closer to the target
    scores higher, and the target itself is the ceiling."""

    return -abs(float(candidate) - TARGET)

def build_components() -> Components:
    """Register the example callables and retain their typed references."""
    registry = Registry()
    proposer = registry.register_proposer(
        "example:propose", "1", propose, deterministic=True, retry_safe=True
    )
    evaluator = registry.register_evaluator(
        "example:evaluate",
        "1",
        evaluate,
        deterministic=True,
        retry_safe=True,
        configuration={"target": TARGET},
    )
    return Components(registry, proposer, evaluator)

def start_run(storage: meta.Storage, components: Components) -> meta.Run:
    """The one run shape used everywhere in this example. Because the run id is
    derived from these inputs, calling ``start_run`` with the same components on
    two different durable paths produces runs with the SAME id."""

    experiment = meta.Experiment(
        task=build_task(components.evaluator),
        seed=0,
        proposer=components.proposer,
        registry=components.registry,
        search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=8),
    )
    return meta.run(experiment, storage=storage, mode="durable-local")

class CrashAfter:
    """Commit-strategy wrapper: perform the first ``n`` commits for real, then
    raise ``SimulatedCrash`` on the next one. Never touches what was committed."""

    def __init__(self, inner: object, *, n: int) -> None:
        self._inner = inner
        self._n = n
        self.commits = 0

    def commit(
        self,
        run_id: RunId,
        expected_version: int,
        *,
        events: Iterable[EventEnvelope],
        occurrences: Iterable[Artifact],
    ) -> int:
        if self.commits >= self._n:
            raise SimulatedCrash(f"simulated process crash after {self._n} committed steps")
        version = self._inner.commit(
            run_id, expected_version, events=events, occurrences=occurrences
        )
        self.commits += 1
        return version

What this proves. The crash left a genuine partial durable stream; resume replayed the committed prefix, found the recovery frontier, re-drove the deterministic search from exactly there, and reached the identical best() — with a byte-identical final event stream. That is the M4 durable-runs guarantee.

The same guarantee holds for runs that use M3 policy-pushed context and pull experience (see tests/test_resume_context.py / tests/test_resume_experience_faults.py).
