docs.title: Crash recovery for durable runs (meta.resume)¶
docs.text:
The central promise of a durable Meta-Evolve run: a process that dies partway through loses no committed work, and once resume-d reaches the exact result an uninterrupted run would have reached.

Interrupted is logically equivalent to uninterrupted.

This notebook walks the lifecycle end to end:

  1. Run a durable-local run to completion, uninterrupted, on path A — its best() is the reference.
  2. Start the same run on path B, but simulate a process crash after a few committed batches.
  3. Reopen path B and resume the run.
  4. Assert the resumed best() equals the uninterrupted reference.

Key concepts: atomic batch commits (a crash leaves only whole batches, never a half-written one), the recovery frontier (resume replays the committed prefix and continues deterministically from the last decided step), and deterministic run identity (the run id is derived from the inputs, so the run on path B shares path A's id and resume can address it).

docs.title: Components — imported from the example module¶
docs.text: durable-local mode requires registered, source-digestible, module-level functions so resume can verify the components it replays are byte-for-byte the ones recorded. Functions defined inside a notebook cell have no resolvable source file, so durable-local would reject them (CapabilityError). We therefore import the real components from examples/operations/crash_recovery/main.py (an importable module) and show their source below — the notebook orchestrates the lifecycle with the example's own building blocks.

docs.title: Simulating a crash — you never write this¶
docs.text:
A real crash (power loss, kill -9, OOM) needs no code; the OS/hardware supplies it. CrashAfter exists only so a deterministic notebook can stand in for one — in production you never author it or touch storage._commit_strategy.

A faithful crash never truncates the append-only store: it just stops committing after some whole batch n, so the n committed batches on disk are exactly what an uninterrupted run would have written, with no partial batch.

docs.title: (1) Uninterrupted reference run on path A¶
docs.text: A counting wrapper with an unreachable threshold rides along to tally path A's own committed batches.

docs.title: (2) Start the same run on path B — then crash mid-way¶
docs.text: The run id matches path A's by construction, so we can resume it by id.

docs.title: (3) Reopen path B and resume(run_id, ...)¶
docs.text: No crash wrapper this time — a fresh durable handle on the same path, exactly as a restarted process would.

docs.title: Advanced examples¶
docs.text: The basic lifecycle resumed from a single mid-run crash. These show the guarantee is total — resume works from every committed boundary — and extends to M3 policy-pushed context and pull experience. All components come from main.py / advanced.py (importable + source-digestible, as durable-local requires).

docs.title: A. Fault matrix — resume from every committed boundary¶
docs.text: Crash after each batch K in turn; each resume reaches the identical best() and a byte-identical final stream.

docs.title: B. The recovery frontier¶
docs.text: resume classifies where the crash left the run (via classify_frontier) before continuing deterministically. The phases seen across boundaries:

docs.title: C. Cold rebuild from empty tables¶
docs.text: A fresh process reopens the durable store; the read model is rebuilt purely from the committed event log — no in-memory state carried over.

docs.title: D. Resumable with M3 policy-pushed context (AncestorsOnly)¶
docs.text: The run records a context-policy manifest, its declaration, and each per-trial selection. resume rebuilds the context policy from the registry and reuses the committed selections — equivalent at every boundary.

docs.title: E. Resumable with M3 pull experience (PullAccess)¶
docs.text: Here the proposer reads experience each step, audited as an attempt then a resolution (two atomic batches). A crash between them leaves a trailing unresolved attempt; resume rolls it forward — recomputing the resolution and reusing the committed operation id — to a byte-identical stream.

docs.title: F. Resume is safe to re-run¶
docs.text: Resuming an already-complete run is a no-op returning the same result. (Two processes racing to resume one crashed run is also safe: exactly one commits and the other gets EventStreamConflict — never a double-commit or partial write. See tests/test_resume_faults.py.)

docs.title: Milestone 5 tour: immutable source, external evidence¶
docs.text: This tour follows the canonical clamp repair in six small steps. The declaration path stays at source, patch, evaluator, budget, and search vocabulary. Returned lineage entries provide optional inspection after the run.

docs.title: 1. Load immutable source¶
docs.text: The source tree contains exact UTF-8 text. The tour stages only the declared tracked candidate/clamp.py bytes into its temporary evidence directory before loading. This isolates the tour from checkout-generated __pycache__ without adding ignore rules: production load_source_tree still rejects every undeclared file.

docs.title: 2. Declare the exact-file repair¶
docs.text: The patch names one file, commits the parent text it expects, and supplies its replacement. A conflict, invalid path, or unchanged replacement is a typed proposal outcome.

docs.title: 3. Declare the independent evaluator¶
docs.text: The grader remains outside the candidate tree, and the fixed run_grader.py owns the exit protocol: exit 0 passes, exit 1 is a rankable task failure, and any other exit is a typed evaluator failure.

docs.title: 4. Declare one budget¶
docs.text: Two evaluations cover the broken seed and one successor. The same budget is passed to the task and run.

docs.title: 5. Run one local Greedy step¶
docs.text: Proposal and evaluation each receive a fresh workspace. Durable storage retains the committed history, while the live local callbacks remain non-portable.

docs.title: 6. Inspect the result and durable boundary¶
docs.text: The public lineage query is progressive disclosure: it returns immutable lineage entries for inspection without putting kernel construction types into the declaration story. Content digests and semantic outcomes are deterministic; observed process wall time is intentionally omitted.

docs.title: Failure boundary: a broken grader is not a low score¶
docs.text: Candidate-caused breakage remains the rankable score 0 seen above. This separate probe removes the grader itself: runner exit 2 becomes EvaluatorFailure, with no metric to rank.

docs.title: Feedback Descent lab

Terminology. A candidate is a meta.Text solver prompt. A pairwise evaluator chooses between two answers and emits textual feedback; an editor derives one successor prompt from that evidence. This is a small teaching implementation inspired by Feedback Descent, not a reproduction of its results or an official SealQA evaluation.

docs.title: Autoresearch, in miniature¶
docs.text: Can an outer Meta-Evolve run improve the recipe used by an inner researcher while private tasks, budgets, and promotion remain outside candidate authority? This notebook executes the deterministic teaching example. The standalone chapter contains the complete explanation.

docs.title: Run the outer loop¶
docs.text: The seed and two successors each receive the same four inner benchmark tasks and the same five-evaluation inner budget. Public task scores are evidence; private quality is the selection metric.

docs.title: Read the evidence boundary¶
docs.text: The proposer derives each edit from a public-report evidence record. Private task details never enter that evidence. Held-out scores are calculated only after result.best() has fixed the selected recipe, and promotion=none is explicit.

docs.title: Change and predict¶
docs.text: Reduce INNER_TRIALS from four to two and update INNER_BUDGET. Predict the selected recipe first. If it changes, did the researcher become worse, or did the evaluation choose a different researcher for a different resource regime?

Status: Shipped. Every entry on this page is generated from the installed meta_evolve package. The four tiers organize the root imports without changing or hiding them.

The namespaced Specialists and TreeSearch presets (meta_evolve.policies.Specialists, meta_evolve.policies.TreeSearch) are documented in the programming model and search guide; neither is a root export.

docs.title: Presentation records
docs.text: Only ArtifactPresentation and ArtifactDiff are root-exported records. Their minimal immutable supporting records live in meta_evolve.presentation: PresentationSection groups labelled PresentationField values and PresentationDocument text; each document has an optional path and explicit truncation state. FileDiff carries its path, added/removed/modified/unchanged status, typed DiffLine values with optional old/new line numbers, and an optional refusal or truncation notice. These records contain inert data only, not HTML, SVG, URLs, or trusted markup.

docs.title: Optional local browser
docs.text: The browser adds no root exports beyond the dependency-free presentation contract above. Install meta-evolve[browser] (or use uv sync --extra browser) and start meta-evolve ui --storage PATH. Its server-rendered routes are documented in the local browser guide.

docs.title: Generated entries
docs.text: The root package keeps the simple callable path small: define a task, bound it with a budget, and state what to maximize or minimize. The full durable vocabulary for policy authors and kernel code lives in meta_evolve.domain, the read-only graph query surface used by context policies is root-exported, and canonical serialization lives in meta_evolve.serialization.

docs.title: CapabilityError
docs.text:
Bases: RunError

A run's declared or requested execution profile is not honored.

Raised for unverifiable component implementations (lambdas, closures, functools.partial, decorated wrappers, or callables with no resolvable module source), unregistered (role, name, version) lookups, and durable-local configuration that lacks a registry, durable storage, or a registered evaluator/proposer/policy. Built-in keys are non-overridable — every codec offered for one is rejected, the built-in object included: a new decode under an old key would change the meaning of every artifact already committed under it, so different behavior needs a new key.

docs.title: resolve_policy(spec, *, budget)
docs.text:
Rebuild a bound program from spec and confirm it round-trips.

Constructs the unbound preset from the registered factory and spec.configuration, binds it against proposer/budget, and asserts the rebuilt SearchSpec equals spec exactly — the same check M4.4's resume relies on (there, budget is the recorded RunStarted.run_budget).

docs.title: Run

docs.title: inspect()
docs.text: Return one immutable aggregate built from one validated replay.

docs.title: trials()
docs.text:
Every committed attempt in commit order, seed trial first.

The winner-shaped queries answer "what came out of this run"; this one answers "what happened in it", so it reports losers, failed proposals, and trials the budget never authorised for evaluation, and it is the one query that never raises NoSuccessfulEvaluation. Read TrialView.state to tell those apart.

docs.title: usage()
docs.text:
Everything this run consumed, including work that failed to rank.

Use this rather than summary().usage whenever a caller is accumulating -- a roll-up over inner runs, or any total that must survive a bad episode. summary() raises NoSuccessfulEvaluation when a run scored nothing, which unwinds the caller and discards the resources already accumulated from earlier episodes as well as this one's. This reports the same figure as inspect().overview.task_usage and never raises for that reason.

A run that does not exist raises RunNotFound, as inspect() does. That is the point of require_existing: without it the unbootstrapped projection leaks a bare SearchNotStarted, and this accessor promises the same answers and the same errors as the aggregate it stands in for.

docs.title: Storage dataclass
docs.text:
Paired artifact and event storage, plus one all-or-none commit.

is_durable and is_read_only are independent capabilities. Durability says committed facts live on durable media; read-only says this handle has no commit authority. A writable durable handle therefore reports True, False while :meth:read_only reports True, True.

docs.title: durable(path) classmethod
docs.text: Wire durable storage into path (created if missing): one SQLite connection (events + artifact occurrence rows) shared with a content-addressed filesystem blob store under path/artifacts.

docs.title: read_only(path) classmethod
docs.text:
Open an existing durable directory with inspection authority only.

The directory and current schema must already exist. This path never creates, stamps, migrates, or otherwise repairs durable state.

docs.title: compose(artifacts, events, *, commit_strategy, close=None) classmethod
docs.text:
Compose independently implemented stores behind one atomic commit.

The strategy declares whether its commit survives process restart; callers cannot separately forge is_durable. Composed storage is always writable: Storage cannot verify that third-party stores genuinely refuse writes, so read-only inspection handles come only from :meth:read_only, which pairs the declaration with stores built to fail closed.

docs.title: commit(run_id, expected_version, *, events, occurrences)
docs.text:
Commit events and occurrences as one all-or-none unit.

EventStreamConflict on a stale expected_version propagates unchanged, and nothing is written. See unit_of_work.py for the per-backend guarantee (durable: one SQLite transaction; in-memory: a locked copy-on-write swap; hand-built pair: local-only fallback).

docs.title: runs()
docs.text:
Every run this storage holds events for, sorted by id.

Identities, not Run objects: opening a run validates and replays its whole stream, and detail is already Run.summary()'s job. A listing exists so those queries stay reachable once the ids have scrolled out of a terminal, so it returns exactly what reopening one needs. The order is lexicographic by id and identical across backends; run ids are content-derived, so it is not chronological.

Enumeration is an optional store capability (ports.RunIndex), declared by implementing it. A paired event store that does not is refused explicitly here — never reported as an empty store, which would be a silent capability downgrade.

docs.title: run_version(run_id)
docs.text:
Maximum committed sequence, or 0 for an unseen run id.

This optional high-water-mark query is intended for polling. Opening a required run remains authoritative and raises RunNotFound when no events exist.

docs.title: without_counts property
docs.text:
The measured resources alone, with the kernel-minted counts dropped.

tokens, spend_micros and wall_seconds are measured -- a component reports what it consumed or was billed. trials and evaluations are minted by the coordinator, which is the only thing entitled to say how much work happened, so a component reporting them is invalid and a nested run's own counts belong to that run.

This is the projection every roll-up needs: total += inner.without_counts carries the money and tokens up while leaving the counts inside. It lives on the type that owns the fields so adding a dimension does not mean finding every caller that happened to enumerate them.

The callback receives opaque seed and optional incumbent handles, immutable configuration, and only expand(parent) / stop(reason) actions. Declare every behavior-affecting value on this decorator; closure capture is rejected so the complete configuration remains identity-visible.

docs.title: Advanced experience provenance
docs.text:
Status: Shipped. This reference follows the outcome-first experience guide.

Pushed and pulled observations enter one ordered ledger. Each entry records the run, occurrence kind and ID, logical step, event sequence, operation, result, and exact usage. A proposal's optional derived_from tuple must be an ordered subsequence of references that this proposer actually observed.

Validation rejects a reference that is missing, duplicated contrary to its ledger position, out of scope, from the future, content-inconsistent, or ordered differently from observation. Rejection is typed invalid output and creates no successor artifact.

Committed context selections and pull audits are facts. Replay rebuilds the experience projection and validates derivation without calling the selector, reader, renderer, proposer, or provider. Logical time—not wall-clock completion— decides what was prior.

This strict layer preserves causal claims while leaving everyday proposals free to declare no derivation. Experience remains bounded, explicit, and unable to change evaluation, budgets, permissions, or promotion.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
This page routes terms to their authoritative contracts and explanations. It does not replace the Programming model, Architecture, or API reference.

Artifact. Immutable versioned candidate content interpreted through an artifact codec. See artifact identity and artifact domains.

Task. The owner-controlled declaration of evaluation, objectives, budget, and permissions. See expanded declarations.

Experiment. The seed, proposer, search, context, experience, randomness, and registry declaration run against a task. See the expanded declarations.

Proposer. A replaceable component allowed to suggest successor content from authorized context. See Write a proposer.

Evaluator. An owner-controlled component that returns metrics, evidence, usage, or a typed failure outside candidate authority. See What evaluation may return.

Search. The policy that chooses which occurrence to expand, retain, or stop on. See Choose search.

Trial. The inspectable record of one seed evaluation or successor attempt, including lineage, metrics or failure, evidence, and usage. See What a run returns.

Run. The result and query surface for one fixed experiment execution. See What a run returns.

Evidence. An authorized observation retained beside a proposal or evaluation, with its authority and provenance intact. See What a proposal may see.

Feedback. Evidence made available to a later proposal and therefore treated as development information. See Give proposals feedback.

Occurrence identity and content identity. Content identity says what the artifact bytes are; occurrence identity says where that content appeared in a particular causal history. See Identity.

Rankability. Whether successful metrics exist for the requested objective, so selection or comparison can defend a numeric ordering. See Rankability comes first.

Typed failure. A non-score outcome preserving why proposal, evaluation, policy, resources, or infrastructure prevented valid measurement. See Poor work is not failed measurement.

NoSuccessfulEvaluation. The exception raised when a winner-shaped query has no successful metrics to rank; recorded trial failures remain inspectable. See Rankability comes first.

docs.title: What evaluation may return
docs.text: The evaluator belongs to the experiment owner, not to the thing being improved. It observes the candidate plus its own authorized environment and returns a measurement or a typed failure. Swapping a proposer must not silently swap the measuring instrument.

docs.title: Three result shapes
docs.text:
For the small callable path, an evaluator may return:

  • one scalar score, which becomes the primary metric;
  • a mapping of named numeric metrics; or
  • an EvaluationResult containing metrics, evidence, usage, or a typed failure.

The richer form is useful when a reviewer needs to see how a score was derived or when provider/process usage must be retained. Signatures and field details belong to the API reference.

docs.title: Checks and rubrics answer different questions
docs.text:
Checks answer objective, mechanically testable questions: an order id is correct, a command exits zero, or a response avoids a prohibited claim. They are reproducible and make good hard content gates.

Rubrics decompose judgment into named criteria such as empathy, action, timeline, and concision. Return the criterion metrics and evaluator-authored evidence alongside the overall metric so disagreement remains inspectable.

A combined evaluator can apply hard gates first and score a rubric only when they pass. A valid gate failure may deliberately return a rankable zero. Keep held-out checks in a separate seed-only run so development feedback cannot leak into the final measurement. The executable pattern is in Grade with checks and rubrics.

docs.title: Poor work is not failed measurement
docs.text:
A valid candidate that performs badly receives metrics and remains rankable. Malformed output, proposer failure, evaluator failure, timeout, resource exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure retain distinct typed outcomes. A broken grader is an EvaluatorFailure, not a candidate score of zero; inventing a score would corrupt selection and comparison.

trials() exposes each state, failure, evidence, and usage, and inspect() works even when every evaluation failed. Winner-shaped queries raise NoSuccessfulEvaluation when no successful evaluation has metrics. That exception describes the impossible query; the recorded failures explain why. See What a run returns for the unrankable path.

docs.title: How the evaluated loop works
docs.text: Evaluated evolution repeats one causal loop: establish a measured baseline, propose a successor, evaluate it independently, let search decide what to do next, and record every outcome. Artifact domains, proposers, evaluators, search, context, and storage remain replaceable without changing that loop.

docs.title: The seed is the baseline
docs.text: Every run starts by encoding and evaluating the seed. That bootstrap consumes one evaluation and no proposal trial. The seed is therefore a measured candidate that search may retain, not an unmeasured default that silently wins when successors fail.

docs.title: Propose, evaluate, search
docs.text:
After bootstrap, each authorized cycle has three distinct decisions:

  1. Search selects an occurrence to expand or stops.
  2. The proposer receives that parent and only the context it is allowed to see.
  3. The evaluator measures a valid successor from outside candidate authority.

The resulting trial records parentage, proposal evidence, evaluation metrics or a typed failure, resource usage, and the search decision. Search may keep an incumbent, retain a population, or request another expansion, but it cannot rewrite a recorded outcome. See Choose search for the shipped policies.

docs.title: Authority stays outside the candidate
docs.text:
The experiment owner declares what better means, what work is allowed, and what limits apply. The coordinator owns evaluation dispatch, accounting, commitment, selection, and stopping. A proposer can suggest artifact content; it cannot change the evaluator, hidden inputs, effective budget, permissions, audit history, or promotion rule. Selecting best() returns a recorded result and never deploys it.

These boundaries keep lineage causal and make failed attempts useful evidence. The full invariant set is owned by the Architecture.

docs.title: The small path lowers to the same loop
docs.text: improve(seed=..., proposer=..., evaluator=..., trials=...) constructs a Task, an Experiment, and Greedy(max_trials=trials), then runs the same coordinator as the expanded declaration. Use the small path for one bounded job; expand it when you need named objectives, a different search policy, context, experience, durable execution, or registered components. The exact contract remains in the Programming model.

docs.title: What a comparison may claim
docs.text:
A comparison is meaningful only when its declarations control the measuring conditions. Run.compare() requires matching evaluator, primary objective, task and effective budget, artifact kind, initial content, and proposer identity. Search, random seed, context, and experience may differ and are reported as the intended variables.

If a protected declaration differs, comparison refuses instead of producing a misleading winner. This is an authority check, not a statistical guarantee: equal declarations can make two records structurally comparable, but they do not prove that a small or noisy sample supports a broad conclusion.

docs.title: Rankability comes first
docs.text:
A run is rankable when at least one successful evaluation produced metrics for the requested objective. Valid poor work, including an intentional hard-gate zero, remains rankable. A trial with only typed failures is not silently placed at the bottom of a numeric ordering.

When a whole run has no successful evaluation, winner-shaped queries such as best() raise NoSuccessfulEvaluation. The exception is a refusal to invent a winner, while trials() and inspect() retain the failures that caused the condition. A run comparison likewise refuses when the requested claim cannot be supported by rankable results.

docs.title: Controlled does not mean fully identified
docs.text: Exact declaration equality is necessary but not magic. A plain closure is identified only by module and qualified name; a captured model id, threshold, or tool policy may be absent from the record. summary().name_only_components makes that limitation visible. Live wrappers should declare all behavior-affecting configuration or use registered component manifests before presenting a comparison as controlled.

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text:
• A cliff-shaped evaluator gives search no useful gradient. Record partial criteria while keeping hard safety gates explicit.
  • Evidence shown to a proposer is development feedback, not held-out evidence.
  • Candidate access to evaluator state or future results invalidates the authority boundary.
  • A closure over a model id or threshold can make two unequal components look identical; configure identity explicitly.
  • Bound the expensive meter and use an objective satisfaction threshold when a known-good result should stop work.
  • None and NoSuccessfulEvaluation are different: an optional value may be absent, while an unrankable run has no defensible winner.

The component playground demonstrates controlled swaps, and Inspect and compare covers the query workflow.
